{{Short description|none}}
Each entry on this list of common misconceptions is worded as a correction; the misconceptions themselves are implied rather than stated. These entries are concise summaries; the main subject articles can be consulted for more detail.

{{Main|List of common misconceptions}}

== Astronomy and spaceflight ==
* There is no scientific evidence that the motion of stars, planets, and other celestial bodies influences the fates of humans, and [[astrology and science|astrology]] has repeatedly been shown to have no explanatory power in predicting future events.<ref name="Cosmic">{{#invoke:cite|book|author1=Jeffrey Bennett |url=https://archive.org/details/astronomymediawo04lopr |title=The cosmic perspective |author2=Megan Donohue |author3=Nicholas Schneider |author4=Mark Voit |publisher=Pearson/Addison-Wesley |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-8053-9283-8 |edition=4th |location=San Francisco, CA |pages=[https://archive.org/details/astronomymediawo04lopr/page/82 82–84] |url-access=registration}}</ref><ref name="Carlson">{{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Carlson |first=Shawn |year=1985 |title=A double-blind test of astrology |url=http://muller.lbl.gov/papers/Astrology-Carlson.pdf |journal=Nature |volume=318 |issue=6045 |pages=419–425 |bibcode=1985Natur.318..419C |doi=10.1038/318419a0 |s2cid=5135208}}</ref><ref name="Zarka">{{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Zarka |first=Philippe |year=2011 |title=Astronomy and astrology |url=https://zenodo.org/record/890932 |journal=Proceedings of the International Astronomical Union |volume=5 |issue=S260 |pages=420–425 |bibcode=2011IAUS..260..420Z |doi=10.1017/S1743921311002602 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
* Astronauts in orbit have the sensation of being [[weightlessness|weightless]] because they are in [[free fall]] around the Earth,<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web| title=freefall | date=December 11, 2023 | quote=An astronaut orbiting Earth in a spacecraft experiences a condition of weightlessness because both the spacecraft and the astronaut are in free fall. |url=https://www.britannica.com/science/freefall-physics}}</ref> not because they are so far away from the Earth that its gravitational pull is negligible. For example, on the [[International Space Station]] the Earth's gravity is nearly 90% as strong as at the surface. Objects orbiting in space would not remain in orbit if not for the gravitational force, and gravitational fields extend infinitely, though the strength of the gravitational force is attenuated with distance.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Oberg|first=James|author-link=James Oberg|date=May 1993|title=Space myths and misconceptions|url=http://www.jamesoberg.com/myth.html|url-status=live|journal=Omni|volume=15|issue=7|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927005829/http://www.jamesoberg.com/myth.html|archive-date=September 27, 2007|access-date=May 2, 2007}}</ref><ref name="nature1">{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Cowen |first1=Ron |title=Andromeda on collision course with the Milky Way |journal=Nature |date=31 May 2012 |doi=10.1038/nature.2012.10765 |s2cid=124815138}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|author=Chandler, David|date=May 1991|title=Weightlessness and Microgravity|url=http://www.lcurve.org/writings/PT-WeightlessnessAndMicrogravity.pdf|journal=The Physics Teacher|volume=29|issue=5|pages=312–13|bibcode=1991PhTea..29..312C|doi=10.1119/1.2343327}}</ref> There is no limit to the distance across which two objects exert gravitational forces upon one another.
* [[File:Back side of the Moon AS16-3021.jpg|thumb|right|The [[far side of the Moon|dark side of the Moon]] directly illuminated by the Sun]] The [[far side of the Moon|dark side of the Moon]] receives about the same amount of light from the [[Sun]] as the [[near side of the Moon|near side]]. Since the same side of the Moon always faces the Earth due to [[tidal locking]], the far side had not been seen until [[Luna 3]] photographed it in 1959. Hence, "dark" refers to the far side being unseen from Earth, not to any lack of illumination by the Sun. <ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|web|last=Sigurdsson|first=Steinn|date=June 9, 2014|title=The Dark Side of the Moon: a Short History|url=http://scienceblogs.com/catdynamics/2014/06/09/the-dark-side-of-the-moon-a-short-history/|access-date=September 16, 2017}} 
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|news|last=Messer|first=A'ndrea Elyse|date=June 9, 2014|title=55-year-old dark side of the moon mystery solved|publisher=Penn State News|url=http://news.psu.edu/story/317841/2014/06/09/research/55-year-old-dark-side-moon-mystery-solved|access-date=September 16, 2017}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|web|last=Falin|first=Lee|date=January 5, 2015|title=What's on the Dark Side of the Moon?|url=http://www.quickanddirtytips.com/education/science/what%E2%80%99s-on-the-dark-side-of-the-moon|access-date=September 16, 2017|archive-date=November 30, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181130124604/https://www.quickanddirtytips.com/education/science/what%E2%80%99s-on-the-dark-side-of-the-moon}}</ref>
* [[Black hole]]s have the same gravitational effects as any other equal mass in their place. They will draw objects towards them according to distance and mass, just as any other celestial body does, except at very close distances to the black hole, comparable to its [[Schwarzschild radius]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|last=Wolfson|first=Richard|title=Simply Einstein: relativity demystified|publisher=W.W. Norton & Co.|date=2002|page=261|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OUJWKdlFKeQC&pg=PA219|isbn=978-0-393-05154-4}}</ref> If, for example, the Sun were replaced by a black hole of equal mass, the orbits of the planets would be essentially unaffected.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://oyc.yale.edu/astronomy/astr-160/lecture-9#transcript |title=Frontiers And Controversies In Astrophysics Lecture 9 |publisher=[[Yale University]] |access-date=April 26, 2011}}</ref>
* [[File:Earth seasons seen as terminator motion.gif|thumb|Earth's [[equator]] does not line up with the [[ecliptic]] ([[orbital plane|plane]] of [[Earth's orbit]]), so for half of the year, the [[Northern Hemisphere]] is tilted more toward the [[Sun]], and for the other half, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted more away, causing [[seasonal lag|seasonal temperature variation]].]] Seasons are not caused by Earth being [[orbital eccentricity|closer to the Sun]] in the summer than in the winter, but by [[effect of Sun angle on climate|the effects]] of Earth's 23.4-degree axial tilt. Each hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun in its respective summer, resulting in longer days and more perpendicular sunlight, with the opposite being true in the winter. Earth reaches [[perihelion|the point in its orbit closest]] to the Sun in January, and it reaches [[apsis|the point farthest]] from the Sun in July, so the [[Season#Elliptical Earth orbit|slight contribution of orbital eccentricity]] opposes the temperature trends of the seasons in the Northern Hemisphere.<ref name="Science@NASA">{{#invoke:cite|web |last=Phillips|first=Tony |date=July 4, 2003 |title=The Distant Sun |url=http://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2002/02jul_aphelion |access-date=April 21, 2021 |publisher=[[NASA]] |archive-date=December 5, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221205153902/https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2002/02jul_aphelion/}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web |url=http://www.adlerplanetarium.org/education/resources/sunearth/section06i.shtml |publisher=Adler Planetarium |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071216004548/http://www.adlerplanetarium.org/education/resources/sunearth/section06i.shtml |archive-date=December 16, 2007 |title=Sun-Earth Connection |access-date=May 8, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web |url=http://istp.gsfc.nasa.gov/istp/outreach/sunearthmiscons.html |title=Ten Things You Thought You Knew about Sun-Earth Science |publisher=NASA |access-date=May 8, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130221092931/http://istp.gsfc.nasa.gov/istp/outreach/sunearthmiscons.html |archive-date=February 21, 2013 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* When a meteor or spacecraft [[atmospheric entry|enters the atmosphere]], the [[Atmospheric entry#Real (equilibrium) gas model|heat of entry]] is not primarily caused by friction, but by [[adiabatic heating|adiabatic compression of air]] in front of the object.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web |url=http://www.nasa.gov/centers/ames/research/2007/faq-shuttleglass_prt.htm |title=NASA – Spacecraft Design |access-date=January 7, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090709055746/http://www.nasa.gov/centers/ames/research/2007/faq-shuttleglass_prt.htm |archive-date=July 9, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web |url=http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/badastronomy/2009/03/30/more-booming-fireballs/ |title=More booming fireballs |work=Bad Astronomy |access-date=January 7, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131215231308/http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/badastronomy/2009/03/30/more-booming-fireballs/ |archive-date=December 15, 2013 |date=March 30, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web |url=http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/badastronomy/2008/12/14/meteor-propter-hoc/ |title=Meteor propter hoc |last=Plait|first=Phil |author-link=Phil Plait |date=December 14, 2008 |work=Bad Astronomy |publisher=Discover |access-date=January 19, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140203034517/http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/badastronomy/2008/12/14/meteor-propter-hoc/ |archive-date=February 3, 2014| url-status=live}}</ref>
* [[Egg balancing]] is possible on every day of the year, not just the [[March equinox|vernal equinox]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web |url=http://www.snopes.com/science/equinox.asp |title=Infernal Egguinox |work=[[Snopes]] |date=March 6, 2012 |access-date=January 29, 2014}}</ref><ref name="AP">{{#invoke:cite|news|url=https://apnews.com/0cf1b28fd3bb7e0efa8f91da775ea6e8|title=Equinox Returns and Eggs Keep Balancing|author=Schmid, Randolph|date=September 20, 1987|access-date=January 29, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140427084100/http://www.apnewsarchive.com/1987/Equinox-Returns-and-Eggs-Keep-Balancing/id-0cf1b28fd3bb7e0efa8f91da775ea6e8|archive-date=April 27, 2014|url-status=live|work=Associated Press News}}</ref> 
* The [[Fisher Space Pen]] was not commissioned by NASA at a cost of millions of dollars, while the Soviets used pencils. Pencils posed a major risk to astronauts due to the release of substances such as shavings and pencil lead being a flight hazard.<ref>{{cite web |title=Space Pen History |url=http://www.allwrite.com/Space-Pen-History.html |access-date=October 4, 2013 |archive-date=October 5, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005005721/http://www.allwrite.com/Space-Pen-History.html | url-status=dead}}</ref> The pen was independently developed by Paul C. Fisher, founder of the Fisher Pen Company, with $1&nbsp;million of his own funds (equivalent to ${{Inflation|US|1|1965}}&nbsp;million in {{Inflation/year|US}}).<ref>[https://www.spacepen.com/about-us.aspx "Fisher Space Pen – Our story"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220108093344/https://www.spacepen.com/about-us.aspx |date=2022-01-08}} Retrieved on February 4, 2019</ref> NASA tested and approved the pen for space use, then purchased 400 pens at $6 per pen ({{Inflation|US|6|1967|fmt=eq}}).<ref>[https://history.nasa.gov/spacepen.html "NASA – The Fisher Space Pen"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220111230216/https://history.nasa.gov/spacepen.html |date=January 11, 2022}} Retrieved on February 4, 2019</ref> The Soviet Union subsequently also purchased the Space Pen for its [[Soyuz (spacecraft)|Soyuz]] spaceflights.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|last=Curtin |first=Ciara |title=Fact or Fiction?: NASA Spent Millions to Develop a Pen that Would Write in Space, whereas the Soviet Cosmonauts Used a Pencil |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/fact-or-fiction-nasa-spen/ |access-date=May 18, 2022 |website=Scientific American |language=en}}</ref>
* [[Tang (drink)|Tang]], [[Velcro]], and [[Teflon]] were not [[NASA spinoff technologies|spun off from technology originally developed by NASA]] for spaceflight, though many other products (such as [[memory foam]] and [[space blanket]]s) were.<ref name="spinfaq">{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://spinoff.nasa.gov/faq|title=Spinoff Frequently Asked Questions |work=NASA.gov|access-date=February 28, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|news|title=Boomers collect artifacts, memories of NASA's heyday |last=Courter |first=Barry |newspaper=[[Times Free Press]] |date=May 13, 2007 |url=http://www.timesfreepress.com/news/2007/may/13/Boomers-collect-artifacts-memories-of-NASAs/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110930222247/http://www.timesfreepress.com/news/2007/may/13/Boomers-collect-artifacts-memories-of-NASAs/ |archive-date=September 30, 2011}}</ref>
* The [[Sun]] is not yellow; rather, it emits light across the full [[Visible spectrum|spectrum of visible colors]], and this combined light appears white when outside of Earth's atmosphere. Earth's atmosphere [[Rayleigh scattering|scatters]] shorter wavelengths of light, particularly blues and violets, more than longer wavelengths like reds and yellows, and this scattering is why the Sun appears yellow during the day or orange or red during sunrise and sunset. The scattered blue/violet light, appearing to come from all directions, is what makes the rest of the sky look blue.<ref name="SunStanford">{{#invoke:cite|web|last1=Scherrer |first1=Deborah |display-authors=etal |title=What Color do YOU think the Sun is? |url=http://solar-center.stanford.edu/SID/activities/GreenSun.html |website=Stanford SOLAR Center |access-date=June 1, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://eclipse2017.nasa.gov/what-color-sun |title=What Color is the Sun? |author=Lou Mayo |website=NASA Eclipse2017 |date=25 May 2023 |access-date=2024-01-24}}</ref>
* [[File:Great Wall of China, Satellite image.jpeg|thumb|right|A satellite image of a section of the [[Great Wall of China]], running diagonally from lower left to upper right (not to be confused with the much more prominent river running from upper left to lower right)]] The [[Great Wall of China]] is not the only [[Artificial structures visible from space|human-made object visible from space]] or from the Moon.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|date=April 2, 2009 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/great-wall/ |title=Great Wall |work=NASA |access-date=July 5, 2024}}</ref> None of the [[List of Apollo astronauts|Apollo astronauts]] reported seeing ''any'' specific human-made object from the Moon, and even Earth-orbiting astronauts can see it only with magnification. City lights, however, are easily visible on the night side of Earth from orbit.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2003/24mar_noseprints/ |title=Space Station Astrophotography |publisher=NASA|date=March 24, 2003|access-date=January 13, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140404162248/https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2003/24mar_noseprints/|archive-date=April 4, 2014|url-status=live}}</ref>
* The [[Big Bang]] model does not fully explain the [[origin of the universe]]. It does not describe how energy, time, and space were caused, but rather it describes the emergence of the present universe from an ultra-dense and high-temperature initial state.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://lweb.cfa.harvard.edu/seuforum/faq.htm#m12 |url-status=live |title=Brief Answers to Cosmic Questions |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=Universe Forum |publisher=[[Harvard–Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics]] |location=Cambridge, MA |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160413195349/https://www.cfa.harvard.edu/seuforum/faq.htm |archive-date=April 13, 2016 |access-date=December 18, 2019}} Archival site: "The Universe Forum's role as part of NASA's Education Support Network concluded in September, 2009."</ref>

== Biology ==
{{See also|Common misunderstandings of genetics}}

=== Mammals ===

* [[Bat#Vision|Bats are not blind]]. While about 70% of bat species, mainly in the [[microbat]] family, use [[animal echolocation|echolocation]] to navigate, all bat species have eyes and are capable of sight. In addition, almost all bats in the [[megabat]] or fruit bat family cannot echolocate and have excellent night vision.<ref name="bats">a. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.nwf.org/News-and-Magazines/National-Wildlife/Animals/Archives/2003/American-Heritage-Animal-Cliches.aspx|title=The Truth About Animal Clichés|date=February 1, 2003|first=Roger|last=Di Silvestro|publisher=National Wildlife Federation|access-date=October 31, 2011}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|title=Blind as a Bat?|format=Press release|publisher=[[Hobart and William Smith Colleges]]|location=Geneva, New York|date=June 12, 2003|url=http://www.collegenews.org/x2682.xml|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080607080055/http://www.collegenews.org/x2682.xml|archive-date=June 7, 2008|access-date=April 7, 2009}}</ref>
* [[File:10 - Cristina Sánchez.jpg|thumb|The color of a red cape does not enrage a bull.|alt=A matador waves a red cape in front of a bull to incite it to charge.]] Bulls are not enraged by the color red, used in capes by [[Bullfighter|professional bullfighters]]. Cattle are [[Dichromacy|dichromats]], so red does not stand out as a bright color. It is not the color of the cape, but the perceived threat by the bullfighter that incites it to charge, along with the spearing of the bull, mental agitation and abuse it endures beforehand.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.itla.net/index.cfm?sec=Longhorn_Information&con=handling|title=Longhorn_Information – handling|first=Larry|last=Smith II|publisher=International Texas Longhorn Association|date=2007|access-date=June 23, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100511090201/http://www.itla.net/index.cfm?sec=Longhorn_Information&con=handling|archive-date=May 11, 2010}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://iacuc.tennessee.edu/pdf/Policies-AnimalCare/Cattle-BasicCare.pdf|title=Cattle – Basic Care|first=A.|last=Dario|date=September 12, 2003|publisher=[[IACUC]], University of Tennessee|access-date=June 23, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080625012822/http://iacuc.tennessee.edu/pdf/Policies-AnimalCare/Cattle-BasicCare.pdf|archive-date=June 25, 2008}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|book|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GhmrNYJhcrIC&pg=PA45|title=The Biology of Animal Stress|editor=Moberg, Gary|editor2=Mench, Joy A.|chapter=Behavioral Principles of Handling Cattle and Other Grazing Animals under Extensive Conditions|first=Temple|last=Grandin|page=45|publisher=[[CAB International|CABI]]|date=2007|isbn=978-1-84593-219-0}}</ref>
* [[Camel#Ecological and behavioral adaptations|Camels]] do not store water in their humps, but rather fatty tissue which can be used as a reserve source of calories. While they can go long periods without water, the water is stored in the animal's bloodstream, not their humps.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.loc.gov/everyday-mysteries/zoology/item/how-much-water-does-a-camels-hump-hold/#:~:text=A%20camel's%20hump%20does%20not,become%20limp%20and%20droop%20down.|publisher=Library of Congress|access-date=2025-05-06|title=How much water does a camel's hump hold?|archive-date=2025-04-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250425133241/https://www.loc.gov/everyday-mysteries/zoology/item/how-much-water-does-a-camels-hump-hold/#:~:text=A%20camel's%20hump%20does%20not,become%20limp%20and%20droop%20down.|url-status=live}}</ref>
* [[Cat|Domestic cats']] behavioral and personality traits cannot be predicted from their coat color. Rather, these traits depend on a complex interplay between genetic and environmental factors.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Udell | first1=Monique | last2=Delgado | first2=Mikel | last3=Ekenstedt | first3=Kari | last4=Shoveller | first4=Anna Kate | last5=Croney | first5=Candace | title=CATastrophic myths part 2: Common misconceptions about the environmental, nutritional, and genetic management of domestic cats and their welfare implications | journal=The Veterinary Journal | volume=300-302 | date=2023 | doi=10.1016/j.tvjl.2023.106029 | article-number=106029| pmid=37683762 | doi-access=free | pmc=13335865 }}</ref>
*Not all cats are attracted and intoxicated by [[catnip]], which affects only about two thirds of them. Alternatives exist, such as [[valerian root]] and leaves.<ref name="bmcvetres.biomedcentral.com">{{cite journal |last1=Bol |first1=Sebastiaan |title=Responsiveness of cats (Felidae) to silver vine (''Actinidia polygama''), Tatarian honeysuckle (''Lonicera tatarica''), valerian (''Valeriana officinalis'') and catnip (''Nepeta cataria'') |journal=BMC Veterinary Research |date=16 March 2017 |doi=10.1186/s12917-017-0987-6 |pmid=28302120 |volume=13 |issue=1 |pmc=5356310 |article-number=70 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Cat World">{{Cite web|title=Catnip (Nepeta cataria) – Everything You Need to Know About Catnip!|url= http://www.cat-world.com.au/all-about-catnip|website=Cat-World.com.au|publisher=Cat World |date=2014 |access-date=2 January 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150206132508/http://www.cat-world.com.au/all-about-catnip |archive-date=6 February 2015}}</ref>
* Dogs do not sweat by [[salivation|salivating]].<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|web|title=Dog noses – myths and facts about your dog's nose – weekly pet tips by Pets.ca|url=http://www.pets.ca/dogs/tips/dog-noses-facts-and-myths-pet-tip-115/|access-date=May 22, 2011}}
<br/>b. {{harvnb|Varasdi|1996|loc=p. 81: "Dogs do not sweat with their tongues as most people believe. They do have some sweat glands, but the ones of most importance are on the pads, or soles, of their feet."}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|book|last=Segaloff|first=Nat|title=The Everything tall tales, legends & outrageous lies book|date=2001|publisher=Adams Media Corp.|isbn=978-1-58062-514-2|page=265|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=03vYAAAAMAAJ|quote=Of course, dogs sweat. You would, too, if you had to wear a fur coat in hot weather. Dogs excrete moisture through the pads on their paws.}}
<br/>d. {{#invoke:cite|book|last=Olien|first=Michael D.|title=The human myth: an introduction to anthropology|date=1978|publisher=Harper & Row|location=New York|isbn=978-0-06-044918-6|page=568|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mvFKAAAAYAAJ|quote=It is another folk tale that dogs do not sweat except through the tongue. This is an incorrect belief as dogs possess sweat glands all over the body.}}
<br/>e. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Aoki|first=T.|author2=Wada, M.|title=Functional Activity of the Sweat Glands in the Hairy Skin of the Dog|journal=Science|date=August 2, 1951|volume=114|issue=2953|pages=123–24|doi=10.1126/science.114.2953.123|bibcode=1951Sci...114..123A|pmid=14854926}}
<br/>f. {{#invoke:cite|journal|title=British Medical Journal 1899 April 15|pmc=2462491 |quote=SOME time ago we received from a correspondent an inquiry as to whether the very prevalent belief that a dog perspires through the tongue was a vulgar error or well founded. ...whether the dog exudes fluid from the tongue of the some kind as that exuded from the human skin. To this question the answer is, No. The skin of the dog is abundantly furnished with glands, having the characteristic disposition and structure of those which in man produce sweat, ... in other words, the dog does not sweat by the tongue.|pages=921–28|volume=1|issue=1998|journal=British Medical Journal|doi=10.1136/bmj.1.1998.921|year=1899}}</ref> Dogs actually do have [[sweat gland]]s, but not on their tongues; they sweat mainly through their footpads. However, dogs do primarily regulate their body temperature through [[thermoregulation|panting]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.petplace.com/dogs/how-do-dogs-sweat/page1.aspx |title=How Do Dogs Sweat|page=1|publisher=Petplace.com |access-date=February 9, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131214113342/http://www.petplace.com/dogs/how-do-dogs-sweat/page1.aspx |archive-date=December 14, 2013|url-status=live}}</ref> (See also: {{Section link|Dog anatomy|Temperature regulation}})
* Dogs do not consistently age seven times as quickly as humans. [[Aging in dogs]] varies widely depending on the breed; certain breeds, such as [[giant dog breeds]] and [[English Bulldog]]s, have much shorter lifespans than average.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cara |first=Ed |date=2023-11-26 |title=The Unhealthiest Dog Breeds |url=https://gizmodo.com.au/2023/11/the-unhealthiest-dog-breeds-2/ |access-date=2024-08-23 |website=Gizmodo Australia |language=en-AU |archive-date=2024-08-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240823151430/https://gizmodo.com.au/2023/11/the-unhealthiest-dog-breeds-2/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Most dogs reach adolescence by one year old; smaller and medium-sized breeds begin to age more slowly in adulthood.<ref>a. Spadafori, Gina (1996). ''Dogs for Dummies''. IDG Books. {{ISBN|978-1-56884-861-7}}
<br/>b. Siegal, Mordecai (Ed.; 1995). ''UC Davis School of Veterinary Medicine Book of the Dogs''; Chapter 5, "Geriatrics", by Aldrich, Janet. Harper Collins. {{ISBN|978-0-06-270136-7}}.
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Wang|first1=Tina|last2=Ma|first2=Jianzhu|last3=Hogan|first3=Andrew N.|last4=Fong|first4=Samson|last5=Licon|first5=Katherine|last6=Tsui|first6=Brian|last7=Kreisberg|first7=Jason F.|last8=Adams|first8=Peter D.|last9=Carvunis|first9=Anne-Ruxandra|last10=Bannasch|first10=Danika L.|last11=Ostrander|first11=Elaine A.|date=July 2, 2020|title=Quantitative Translation of Dog-to-Human Aging by Conserved Remodeling of the DNA Methylome|journal=Cell Systems|volume=11|language=en|issue=2|pages=176–185.e6|doi=10.1016/j.cels.2020.06.006|pmid=32619550|pmc=7484147|issn=2405-4712|doi-access=free}}</ref>
* Old elephants near death do not leave their herd to go to an "[[elephants' graveyard]]" to die.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|news|last=Spanney |first=Laura |date=January 28, 1995 |title=Not many people know that |url=http://www.newscientist.com/article/mg14519625.100-not-many-people-know-that.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080325155037/http://www.newscientist.com/article/mg14519625.100-not-many-people-know-that.html |archive-date=March 25, 2008 |access-date=June 16, 2024 |work=[[New Scientist]]}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://planetwild.com/blog/african-savanna-elephant|date=December 6, 2023|title=Are elephants afraid of mice? Facts and myths about the African savanna elephant|access-date=June 25, 2024 |quote=Mythbusting: Popular myths about the African elephant... Myth: Elephants go to elephant graveyards to die}}</ref>
* The hippopotamus does not produce pink milk, nor does it sweat blood. The skin secretions of the hippopotamus are red due to the presence of [[hipposudoric acid]], a red pigment which acts as a natural sunscreen, and is neither sweat nor blood. It does not affect the color of their milk, which is white or beige.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=FACT CHECK: Is Hippopotamus Milk Pink?|url=https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/false-hippopotamus-milk-pink/|date=January 6, 2016|website=[[Snopes]]|language=en-US|access-date=February 16, 2022}}</ref>
* Lemmings [[Lemming#Misconceptions|do not engage in mass suicide]] by diving off cliffs. The idea was popularized by the 1958 [[Disney]] documentary film ''[[White Wilderness (film)|White Wilderness]]'', in which the lemmings were repeatedly shoved off a cliff by the filmmakers to create the illusion of a mass suicide.<ref name="Mikkelson 2007">{{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.snopes.com/disney/films/lemmings.asp|title=White Wilderness Lemmings Suicide|website=[[Snopes]]|date=August 19, 2007 |first=Barbara and David P. |last=Mikkelson|access-date=August 29, 2009}}</ref><ref name="TotalLemmingDeath">{{#invoke:cite|web|last1=Smith |first1=Nadine |title=How Disney Tricked the World Into Believing Lemmings Commit Mass Suicide |url=https://hyperallergic.com/545742/white-wilderness-disney-nature-documentary/ |website=Hyperallergic |date=March 13, 2020 |access-date=23 August 2022}}</ref> The misconception itself is much older, dating back to at least the late 19th century, though its exact origins are uncertain.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Scott|first=W.|journal=The Monthly Chronicle of North-country Lore and Legend|date=November 1891|title=The Monthly chronicle of North-country lore and legend: v. 1–5; Mar. 1887–Dec. 1891|volume=5|page=523|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=W8rUAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA523}}</ref><ref name="Mikkelson 2007"/>
* [[Mouse#Diet|Mice do not have a special appetite for cheese]], and will eat it only for lack of better options; they actually favor sweet sugary foods. The myth may have come from the fact that before the advent of refrigeration, cheese was usually stored outside and was therefore a food easy for mice to reach.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://animals.howstuffworks.com/animal-facts/do-mice-really-love-cheese.htm|title=Do mice really love cheese?|date=April 15, 2015|website=HowStuffWorks|language=en|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref>
* [[Porcupine#Quills|Porcupines do not shoot their quills]]. They can detach, and porcupines will deliberately back into attackers to impale them, but their quills do not project.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|title=Encyclopædia Britannica: Or, A Dictionary of Arts, Sciences, and Miscellaneous Literature, Enlarged and Improved|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Is0nAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA501|year=1823|publisher=Archibald Constable|pages=501–}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|author=Shepard, Thomas Goodwin|title=The natural history of secession|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MTA5AAAAMAAJ&pg=PA78|year=1865|publisher=Derby & Miller|pages=78–}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://tpwd.texas.gov/publications/nonpwdpubs/introducing_mammals/porcupines/|title=Porcupines|date=n.d.|website=Texas Parks & Wildlife|language=en|access-date=October 14, 2022}}</ref>
* [[Rabbit#Modern times|Rabbits are not especially partial to carrots]]. Their diet in the wild primarily consists of dark green vegetables such as grasses and clovers, and excessive carrot consumption is unhealthy for them due to containing high levels of sugar.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|news|last=Bittel|first=Jason|title=Think you know what bunnies and bears eat? Their diets may surprise you. |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/kidspost/think-you-know-what-bunnies-and-bears-eat-their-diets-may-surprise-you/2019/09/20/bac528ea-ce5d-11e9-87fa-8501a456c003_story.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190926235234/https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/kidspost/think-you-know-what-bunnies-and-bears-eat-their-diets-may-surprise-you/2019/09/20/bac528ea-ce5d-11e9-87fa-8501a456c003_story.html |newspaper=Washington Post|date= September 22, 2019 |archive-date=September 26, 2019|url-status=live|quote=In the wild, rabbits aren't in the habit of digging up root vegetables such as carrots, potatoes and beets. They much prefer wild greens, such as grasses and clover. In fact, carrots may actually be bad for rabbits, because although the vegetables are high in good nutrients, including beta carotene, they are also relatively high in sugar. This means that feeding a rabbit lots of carrots could lead to tooth decay or other health issues.}}</ref> 
* Tomato juice and sauce are ineffective at neutralizing the odor of a [[skunk]]. Rather, due to [[olfactory fatigue]], a person sprayed by a skunk loses sensitivity to the smell over time.<ref>Cosier, Susan (July 26, 2006). [http://scienceline.org/2006/07/ask-cosier-skunk/ Is it true that tomato sauce will get rid of the smell of a skunk?] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221021083131/http://scienceline.org/2006/07/ask-cosier-skunk/ |date=2022-10-21}}. Scienceline. Retrieved on April 5, 2012.</ref> [[Skunk#Mitigation|Effective treatments]] for skunk odor involve artificial compounds rather than household remedies.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web| url = http://www.humanesociety.org/animals/dogs/tips/de-skunking_dog.html |title=De-skunking your dog | publisher = [[The Humane Society of the United States]] | access-date = August 8, 2019 |archive-date=December 10, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161210154906/http://www.humanesociety.org/animals/dogs/tips/de-skunking_dog.html}}</ref>
* There is no such thing as an "[[alpha (ethology)|alpha]]" in a wolf pack. An early study that coined the term "alpha wolf" had observed only unrelated adult wolves living in captivity. In the wild, wolf packs operate like families: parents are in charge until the young grow up and start their own families, and younger wolves do not overthrow an "alpha" to become the new leader.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://apdt.com/pet-owners/choosing-a-trainer/dominance/ |title=Dominance and Dog Training|access-date=January 30, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202064934/https://apdt.com/pet-owners/choosing-a-trainer/dominance/ |archive-date=February 2, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|news|url=http://io9.gizmodo.com/why-everything-you-know-about-wolf-packs-is-wrong-502754629|title=Why everything you know about wolf packs is wrong|last=Davis|first=Lauren|work=io9|date=12 May 2013 |access-date=October 13, 2017|language=en-US}}</ref>
* The [[Lunar phase|phases of the Moon]] have no effect on the [[Wolf communication|vocalizations of wolves]], and wolves do not howl at the Moon.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|last1=Busch|first1=R. H.|title=Wolf Almanac, New and Revised: A Celebration Of Wolves And Their World|publisher=[[Rowman & Littlefield]]|edition=3rd|year=2007|isbn=978-1-59921-069-8|url={{Google books|plainurl=yes|id=svbnCwAAQBAJ}}}}, p. 59</ref> Wolves howl to assemble the pack usually before and after hunts, to pass on an alarm particularly at a den site, to locate each other during a storm, while crossing unfamiliar territory, and to communicate across great distances.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|last=Lopez |first=Barry H. |title=Of Wolves and Men |publisher=J. M. Dent and Sons Limited |year=1978 |isbn=978-0-7432-4936-2 |url={{Google books|plainurl=yes|id=sz8gAQAAIAAJ}}}}, p. 38</ref>

=== Birds ===
* A human touching or handling eggs or baby birds will not cause the adult birds to abandon them.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/a-bird-in-the-hand/ |title=Fact Check: Will Baby Birds Be Rejected by Their Mother If You Handle Them? |first=Barbara |last=Mikkelson |date=August 26, 2001 |website=[[Snopes]]}}</ref> The same is generally true for other animals having their young touched by humans as well, with the possible exception of rabbits (as rabbits will sometimes abandon their nest after an event they perceive as traumatizing).<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/fact-or-fiction-birds-abandon-young-at-human-touch/ |magazine=[[Scientific American]] |title=Fact or Fiction?: Birds (and Other Critters) Abandon Their Young at the Slightest Human Touch |first=Robynne |last=Boyd |date=July 26, 2007}}</ref>
* Eating rice, yeast, or [[Alka-Seltzer]] does not cause birds to explode and is rarely fatal. Birds can [[flatulate]] and [[Regurgitation (digestion)|regurgitate]] to expel gas, and some birds even include wild rice as part of their diet.<ref name="Mikkelson 2000"/><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|last=Mikkelson |first=David |date=2020-05-10 |title=Duck Eats Yeast, Quacks, Explodes; Man Loses Eye |url=https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/duck-eats-yeast-quacks-explodes-man-loses-eye/ |access-date=2023-12-06 |website=[[Snopes]] |language=en}}</ref> The misconception has often led to weddings using [[millet]], [[confetti]], or other materials to shower the newlyweds as they leave the ceremony, instead of the [[Wedding customs by country|throwing of rice]] that is traditional in some places.<ref name="Mikkelson 2000">{{cite web |last1=Mikkelson |first1=Barbara |title=Is Throwing Rice at Weddings Bad for Birds? |url=https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/against-the-grain/ |website=Snopes |access-date=29 July 2024 |date=14 May 2000}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.livescience.com/32624-does-wedding-rice-make-birds-explode.html |title=Does Wedding Rice Make Birds Explode? |date=June 4, 2010 |website=[[Live Science]] |access-date=April 17, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|news|url=https://www.jacksonville.com/story/news/reason/2016/10/19/fact-check-birds-really-can-eat-rice-safely/15728451007/ |work=[[The Florida Times-Union]] |date=October 19, 2016 |title=Fact Check: Birds really can eat rice safely |first=Carole |last=Fader}}</ref>
* [[Bird intelligence|Birds are not stupid]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Describing Someone as "Birdbrained" Is Misguided, Unless You're Talking About Emus |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/describing-someone-birdbrained-misguided-unless-youre-talking-about-emus-180958981/ |access-date=2026-08-31 |website=Smithsonian Magazine |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-08-28 |title=Five species that show why 'bird brain' is a stupid phrase {{!}} Science News |url=https://www.sciencenews.org/blog/wild-things/five-species-show-why-bird-brain-stupid-phrase |access-date=2026-08-31 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-12-02 |title=Bird-Brained Fact or Fiction: How Intelligent are Birds? - Nature Roamer |url=https://natureroamer.com/intelligent-birds/ |access-date=2026-08-31 |language=en-US}}</ref> A wide variety of cognitive abilities have been observed in birds, particularly [[Corvidae|corvids]] and [[Parrot|parrots]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Emery |first=Nathan J. |date=2006-01-29 |title=Cognitive ornithology: the evolution of avian intelligence |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological Sciences |volume=361 |issue=1465 |pages=23–43 |doi=10.1098/rstb.2005.1736 |issn=0962-8436 |pmc=1626540 |pmid=16553307}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Güntürkün |first1=Onur |last2=Bugnyar |first2=Thomas |date=April 2016 |title=Cognition without Cortex |journal=Trends in Cognitive Sciences |volume=20 |issue=4 |pages=291–303 |doi=10.1016/j.tics.2016.02.001 |issn=1879-307X |pmid=26944218}}</ref> [[Tool use by non-human animals|Tool use]] is also present in [[Woodpecker finch|woodpecker finches]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sabine |first1=Tebbich |last2=Irmgard |first2=Teschke |last3=Erica |first3=Cartmill |last4=Sophia |first4=Stankewitz |date=February 2012 |title=Use of a barbed tool by an adult and a juvenile woodpecker finch (Cactospiza pallida) |journal=Behavioural Processes |volume=89 |issue=2 |pages=166–171 |doi=10.1016/j.beproc.2011.10.016 |issn=1872-8308 |pmid=22085790}}</ref>
