Much of the deep web consists of academic libraries, databases, and anything that is not indexed by normal search engines, including most private email accounts and direct messages.<ref>a. {{cite magazine |last1=Greenberg |first1=Andy |title=Hacker Lexicon: What Is the Dark Web? |url=https://www.wired.com/2014/11/hacker-lexicon-whats-dark-web/ |magazine=Wired |access-date=2024-12-26 |archive-date=2015-06-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150607062159/http://www.wired.com/2014/11/hacker-lexicon-whats-dark-web/ |url-status=live}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|last=Callaghan|first=Greg|url=https://www.smh.com.au/technology/the-dark-web-uncovering-monsters-and-myths-in-the-net-s-evil-twin-20180307-p4z39d.html|title=The dark web: uncovering monsters (and myths) in the Net's 'evil twin'|website=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]]|date=March 9, 2018|access-date=August 8, 2022}}
<br/>c. {{cite magazine |last1=Cox |first1=Joseph |date=June 18, 2015 |title=The Dark Web as You Know It Is a Myth |url=https://www.wired.com/2015/06/dark-web-know-myth/ |access-date=August 8, 2022 |magazine=Wired |archive-date=April 3, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230403231231/https://www.wired.com/2015/06/dark-web-know-myth/ |url-status=live}}
<br/>d. {{#invoke:cite|web|last1=Beckett|first1=Andy|title=The dark side of the internet|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2009/nov/26/dark-side-internet-freenet/|website=The Guardian|date=November 25, 2009|access-date=August 8, 2022}}</ref>
* [[Private browsing]] (such as [[Google Chrome|Chrome]]'s "Incognito Mode") does not protect users from being [[Web tracking|tracked]] by websites, governments, or one's [[internet service provider]] (ISP), nor does it hide one's information when using devices or networks owned or maintained by one's employer, school, or other entity, such as a coffee shop. Such entities can still use information such as [[IP address]]es and [[user accounts]] to uniquely identify users.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.fastcompany.com/90311396/incognito-mode-wont-keep-you-private-try-browser-compartmentalization|title=Incognito mode won't keep your browsing private. Do this instead |last=Grothaus |first=Michael|date=April 12, 2019|website=Fast Company|language=en-US|access-date=August 14, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.privacyflake.com/2018/08/incognito-mode-browsing-myths.html|title=Incognito mode while browsing – Myths Busted |first=Anirudh |last=B|work=Privacyflake |access-date=September 6, 2019|archive-date=May 16, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200516215450/https://www.privacyflake.com/2018/08/incognito-mode-browsing-myths.html}}</ref> Private browsing also does not provide additional protection against viruses or malware.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|title=Proceedings of the 2018 World Wide Web Conference: Your Secrets Are Safe: How Browsers' Explanations Impact Misconceptions About Private Browsing Mode|url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3178876.3186088|first1=Yuxi|last1=Wu|first2=Panya|last2=Gupta|first3=Miranda|last3=Wei|first4=Yasemin|last4=Acar|first5=Sascha|last5=Fahl|first6=Blase|last6=Ur|date=23 April 2018|isbn=978-1-4503-5639-8|publisher=International World Wide Web Conferences Steering Committee|location=Republic and Canton of Geneva, CHE in Lyon, France|doi=10.1145/3178876.3186088|pages=217–226|series=WWW '18|s2cid=4881375}}</ref> It is usually only a feature to not record browsing and searching history on the browser.
* [[Phone repair with rice|Submerging a phone in rice]] after it has suffered from water damage has not been shown to be effective in repairing it.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|last=Zelenko |first=Michael |date=September 14, 2015 |title=Putting your wet phone in rice probably won't save it. But do it anyway |url=https://www.theverge.com/2015/9/14/9326035/can-rice-actually-save-your-wet-phone |access-date=March 18, 2022 |website=[[The Verge]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|last=Chugh |first=Ritesh |title=Phone wet and won't turn on? Here's how to deal with water damage (hint: soaking it in rice won't work) |url=http://theconversation.com/phone-wet-and-wont-turn-on-heres-how-to-deal-with-water-damage-hint-soaking-it-in-rice-wont-work-158633 |access-date=March 18, 2022 |website=[[The Conversation (website)|The Conversation]] |date=April 8, 2021 |language=en}}</ref> Even if submerging them in a desiccant were more effective than leaving them to dry in open air, common desiccants such as silica gel or cat litter are better than rice.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|last=Aguilar |first=Nelson |url=https://smartphones.gadgethacks.com/how-to/myth-debunked-uncooked-rice-isnt-best-way-save-your-water-damaged-phone-0154799/ |title=Myth Debunked: Uncooked Rice Isn't the Best Way to Save Your Water-Damaged Phone « Smartphones :: Gadget Hacks |publisher=Smartphones.gadgethacks.com |date=April 30, 2014 |access-date=May 16, 2022}}</ref>
* [[Mobile phone]]s do not create considerable [[electromagnetic interference]] when [[Mobile phone#In hospitals|used in hospitals]].<ref name="Vreeman 2007">Rachel C. Vreeman, Aaron E. Carroll, "Medical Myths", ''[[The British Medical Journal]]'' (now called ''The BMJ'') '''335''':1288 (December 20, 2007), {{doi|10.1136/bmj.39420.420370.25}}</ref>
* The [[Apple logo]] was not inspired by [[Alan Turing]] or his death by [[cyanide]]-laced apple.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/apple-logo |title=The Apple logo: Inside the design of the iconic corporate symbol |last=Sweeney |first=Erica |work=Business Insider |date=January 5, 2024 |access-date=June 6, 2025 |archive-date=June 6, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250606225756/https://www.businessinsider.com/apple-logo |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.manchestersfinest.com/articles/manchester-myths-apple-logo-alan-turing/ |title=Myths of Manchester: The Apple Logo & Alan Turing |last=Brown |first=Ben |work=Manchester's Finest |date=July 25, 2022 |access-date=June 6, 2025 |archive-date=June 6, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250606223122/https://www.manchestersfinest.com/articles/manchester-myths-apple-logo-alan-turing/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Although Turing was found dead with a half-eaten apple near his bed in 1954 and was a key figure in computing history, Apple's logo designer [[Rob Janoff]] has repeatedly denied any connection.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Raszl |first=Ivan |date=July 30, 2020 |title=Interview with Rob Janoff, designer of the Apple logo |url=http://creativebits.org/interview/interview_rob_janoff_designer_apple_logo |access-date=June 6, 2025 |archive-date=August 4, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090804065738/http://creativebits.org/interview/interview_rob_janoff_designer_apple_logo |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Earth and environmental sciences ==
{{See also|Tornado myths}}
[[File:Common Era Temperature.svg|thumb|left|[[Global surface temperature]] reconstruction over the last 2000 years using proxy data from tree rings, corals, and ice cores in blue.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Neukom |first1=Raphael |last2=Barboza |first2=Luis A. |last3=Erb |first3=Michael P. |last4=Shi|first4=Feng |last5=Emile-Geay|first5=Julien |last6=Evans|first6=Michael N. |last7=Franke|first7=Jörg |last8=Kaufman|first8=Darrell S. |last9=Lücke|first9=Lucie |last10=Rehfeld|first10=Kira |last11=Schurer|first11=Andrew |date=2019 |title=Consistent multidecadal variability in global temperature reconstructions and simulations over the Common Era |journal=Nature Geoscience |volume=12 |issue=8 |pages=643–649|doi=10.1038/s41561-019-0400-0|pmid=31372180 |pmc=6675609 |bibcode=2019NatGe..12..643P |issn=1752-0908}}</ref> Directly observed data is in red.<ref name="nasa temperatures">{{#invoke:cite|web|title=Global Annual Mean Surface Air Temperature Change |publisher=NASA |url=https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/graphs_v4/ |access-date=February 23, 2020}}</ref>]]
* Contemporary [[global warming]] is [[Human impact on the environment|driven by human activities]],<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Powell |first1=James |date=November 20, 2019 |title=Scientists Reach 100% Consensus on Anthropogenic Global Warming |journal=Bulletin of Science, Technology & Society |volume=37 |issue=4 |pages=183–184 |doi=10.1177/0270467619886266 |s2cid=213454806}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Lynas |first1=Mark|author2-link=Benjamin Z. Houlton|last2=Houlton |first2=Benjamin Z.|last3=Perry |first3=Simon |date=2021 |title=Greater than 99% consensus on human caused climate change in the peer-reviewed scientific literature |journal=Environmental Research Letters|volume=16 |issue=11|at=114005 |doi=10.1088/1748-9326/ac2966 |bibcode=2021ERL....16k4005L|s2cid=239032360|issn=1748-9326|doi-access=free}}</ref> despite claims that it is [[Climate change denial|not occurring]], [[Global warming conspiracy theory|lacks strong scientific consensus]], or that warming is [[Global warming controversy|mostly caused by non-human factors]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|publisher=Pew Research Center |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2015/01/29/public-and-scientists-views-on-science-and-society/ |title=Public and Scientists' Views on Science and Society|date=January 29, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|author=Lydia Saad |url=https://news.gallup.com/poll/355427/americans-concerned-global-warming.aspx |title=Are Americans Concerned About Global Warming?|publisher=Gallup|date=October 5, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |last=Begley |first=Sharon |author-link=Sharon Begley |date=August 13, 2007 |title=The Truth About Denial |url=http://www.newsweek.com/id/32482 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071021024942/http://www.newsweek.com/id/32482 |archive-date=October 21, 2007 |magazine=[[Newsweek]]}} ([https://web.archive.org/web/20070820002929/http://www.msnbc.msn.com/id/20122975/site/newsweek/page/0/ MSNBC single page version, archived 20 August 2007])</ref> No scientific body of national or international standing disagrees with the decades-old, near-complete [[scientific consensus on climate change]].<ref>a. {{cite report |title=Understanding and responding to climate change: Highlights of National Academies Reports, 2008 edition |year=2008 |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |page=2 |url=http://dels.nas.edu/resources/static-assets/materials-based-on-reports/booklets/climate_change_2008_final.pdf |access-date=November 9, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171011182257/http://dels.nas.edu/resources/static-assets/materials-based-on-reports/booklets/climate_change_2008_final.pdf |archive-date=October 11, 2017}}<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|book|chapter=The scientific consensus on climate change: How do we know we're not wrong? |last1=Oreskes |first1=Naomi |author1-link=Naomi Oreskes |title=Climate Change: What It Means for Us, Our Children, and Our Grandchildren |editor-last1=DiMento |editor-first1=Joseph F. C. |editor-last2=Doughman |editor-first2=Pamela M. |publisher=The MIT Press |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-262-54193-0 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=PXJIqCkb7YIC&pg=PA68 68]}}<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|news|last1=Gleick |first1=Peter |title=Statements on Climate Change from Major Scientific Academies, Societies, and Associations (January 2017 update) |date=January 7, 2017 |work=ScienceBlogs |access-date=April 2, 2020|url=https://scienceblogs.com/significantfigures/index.php/2017/01/07/statements-on-climate-change-from-major-scientific-academies-societies-and-associations-january-2017-update}}</ref> Global warming is primarily a result of the increase in atmospheric [[greenhouse gas]] concentrations (like [[Carbon dioxide|CO<sub>2</sub>]] and [[methane]]) via the [[Industrial Revolution|burning]] of [[fossil fuel]]s as well as other [[Anthropogenic hazard|human activities]] such as [[Deforestation and climate change|deforestation]], with secondary [[climate change feedback]] mechanisms (such as the [[Ice–albedo feedback|melting of the polar ice increasing the Earth's absorption of sunlight]]) assisting to perpetuate the change.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|news|url=https://www.un.org/en/global-issues/climate-change|title=Climate Change|newspaper=United Nations}}</ref>
* [[File:Area of the ozone hole.jpg|thumb|[[Ozone depletion]] is not a cause of [[global warming]].]] Global warming is not caused by the [[Ozone depletion|hole in the ozone layer]]. Ozone depletion is a separate problem caused by [[chlorofluorocarbon]]s (CFCs)<ref name="Jacob">Jacob, Daniel J. ''Introduction to Atmospheric Chemistry''. pp. 177–87. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1999.</ref> which have been released into the atmosphere.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=Chlorofluorocarbons |website=Greenhouse Gases |publisher=NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information |url=https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/monitoring-references/faq/greenhouse-gases.php?section=cfc |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150830030045/https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/monitoring-references/faq/greenhouse-gases.php?section=cfc |archive-date=August 30, 2015 |access-date=October 21, 2018}}</ref> CFCs are strong greenhouse gases;<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://blogs.nasa.gov/whatonearth/tag/cfcs/ |title=CFCS – What on Earth|date=February 24, 2010}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/guides/z3bbb9q/revision/3 |title=The enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming – Physical and human causes of climate change – Higher Geography Revision |website=BBC Bitesize |date=January 1, 1970 |access-date=February 9, 2022}}</ref> however, the hole in the ozone layer is shrinking and in 2019 was the smallest it had been since 1982,<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|date=2019-10-21 |title=2019 Ozone Hole is the Smallest on Record Since Its Discovery – NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers-and-facilities/goddard/2019-ozone-hole-is-the-smallest-on-record-since-its-discovery/ |access-date=2024-04-14 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|news|last=Ansari |first=Talal |title=Ozone Hole Above Antarctica Shrinks to Smallest Size on Record |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/ozone-hole-above-antarctica-shrinks-to-smallest-size-on-record-11571847944 |access-date=2024-04-14 |work=The Wall Street Journal |date=23 October 2019 |language=en-US}}</ref> while global warming continues.
* [[File:Cows and cooling towers, Cottam - geograph.org.uk - 450176.jpg|thumb|upright|Cooling towers from a coal-fired power plant. The white clouds are harmless water vapor from the cooling process.]] [[Cooling tower]]s in [[power station]]s and other facilities do not emit smoke, harmful fumes, or radiation; they emit water vapor and do not contribute to climate change.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|date=February 15, 2007 |title=Myth of cooling towers is symptomatic of global warming information shortage |url=https://www.rsc.org/news-events/articles/2007/02-february/cooling-towers/ |access-date=March 2, 2022 |website=[[Royal Society of Chemistry]] |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web| url=https://climate.mit.edu/ask-mit/why-do-we-blame-climate-change-carbon-dioxide-when-water-vapor-much-more-common-greenhouse | title=Why do we blame climate change on carbon dioxide, when water vapor is a much more common greenhouse gas? &#124; MIT Climate Portal}}</ref>
* [[File:5-Bar-chart-–-What-is-the-safest-form-of-energy.png|thumb|Death rates from air pollution and accidents related to energy production, measured in deaths per terawatt hours (TWh) (left). Carbon emissions measured in tons per gigawatt hour (GWh) (right).]] [[Nuclear power]] is [[Nuclear power#Safety|one of the safest sources of energy]], resulting in orders of magnitude fewer deaths than conventional power sources per unit of energy produced. Extremely few people are killed or injured due to nuclear power on a yearly basis.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|last=Energy |first=Duke |title=Common Myths About Nuclear Energy |url=https://nuclear.duke-energy.com/2013/06/12/common-myths-about-nuclear-energy |access-date=2023-04-23 |website=Duke Energy {{!}} Nuclear Information Center |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=10 myths about nuclear energy {{!}} Argonne National Laboratory |url=https://www.anl.gov/article/10-myths-about-nuclear-energy |access-date=2023-04-23 |website=www.anl.gov |date=September 9, 2013 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=What are the safest sources of energy? |url=https://ourworldindata.org/safest-sources-of-energy |access-date=2020-05-27 |website=Our World in Data|date=10 February 2020 |last1=Ritchie |first1=Hannah}}</ref><ref name="Frank N. von Hippel 27–36">{{#invoke:cite|journal|author=Frank N. von Hippel |date=September–October 2011 |title=The radiological and psychological consequences of the Fukushima Daiichi accident |url=http://bos.sagepub.com/content/67/5/27.full |journal=Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists |volume=67 |issue=5 |pages=27–36 |bibcode=2011BuAtS..67e..27V |doi=10.1177/0096340211421588 |s2cid=218769799}}</ref> (See also: [[Radiophobia]])
* [[Earthquake]] strength (or magnitude) is not commonly measured using the [[Richter scale]]. Although the Richter scale was used ''historically'' to measure earthquake magnitude (not [[Modified Mercalli intensity scale|earthquake damage]]), it was found in the 1970s that it does not reliably represent the magnitude of large earthquakes. It has therefore been largely replaced by the [[moment magnitude scale]],<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|date=2016-04-28 |title=USGS Earthquake Magnitude Policy (implemented on January 18, 2002) |url=http://earthquake.usgs.gov:80/aboutus/docs/020204mag_policy.php |access-date=2023-11-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160428095841/http://earthquake.usgs.gov:80/aboutus/docs/020204mag_policy.php |archive-date=April 28, 2016}}</ref> although very small earthquakes are still sometimes measured using the Richter scale.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=British Geological Survey Seismology Monitoring Page |url=https://www.earthquakes.bgs.ac.uk/education/faqs/faq15.html |access-date=2023-11-08 |website=www.earthquakes.bgs.ac.uk}}</ref> Nevertheless, earthquake magnitude is still widely misattributed to the Richter scale.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|date=2011-05-10 |title=Explained: Measuring earthquakes |url=https://news.mit.edu/2011/exp-measuring-earthquakes-0510 |access-date=2023-11-08 |website=MIT News {{!}} Massachusetts Institute of Technology |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|last=Reich |first=Kenneth |date=1988-02-29 |title=Science / Medicine: The Richter Scale: Caltech Seismologists Say Temblor Rating Has a Magnitude of Problems |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-02-29-me-179-story.html |access-date=2023-11-08 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|date=2015-05-15 |title=What are the faultlines with the Richter scale? |url=https://www.euronews.com/2015/05/15/what-are-the-faultlines-with-the-richter-scale |access-date=2023-11-08 |website=euronews |language=en}}</ref>
* [[Lightning]] can, and often does, strike the same place twice. Lightning in a thunderstorm is more likely to strike objects and spots that are more prominent or conductive. For instance, lightning strikes the [[Empire State Building]] in [[New York City]] on average 23 times per year.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-myths|title=Lightning Myths and Facts|publisher=National Weather Service|quote=Fact: Lightning often strikes the same place repeatedly, especially if it's a tall, pointy, isolated object. The Empire State Building is hit an average of 23 times a year}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|title=Lightning Often Strikes Twice|work=NASA Spinoff|publisher=Office of the Chief Technologist, NASA|url=http://www.sti.nasa.gov/tto/Spinoff2005/ps_3.html|access-date=June 23, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120325015918/http://www.sti.nasa.gov/tto/Spinoff2005/ps_3.html|archive-date=March 25, 2012}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|web|author=WeatherBug Meteorologists|title=The Myths and Facts of Lightning|website=WeatherBug|url=http://weather.weatherbug.com/weather-news/weather-reports.html?story=6571|publisher=Earth Works|date=May 17, 2010|access-date=June 23, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100711061017/http://weather.weatherbug.com/weather-news/weather-reports.html?story=6571|archive-date=2010-07-11|url-status=live}}
<br/>d. {{#invoke:cite|web|author=Tristan Simpson|date=Apr 29, 2022|url=https://www.theweathernetwork.com/ca/news/article/can-lightning-strike-the-same-place-twice|title=Can lightning strike the same place twice?|website=The Weather Network}}</ref>
* [[Heat lightning]] does not exist as a distinct phenomenon. What is mistaken for "heat lightning" is usually ordinary lightning from storms too distant to hear the associated [[thunder]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=What Is Heat Lightning?|date=18 August 2016 |url=https://weather.com/science/weather-explainers/news/heat-lightning-explainer |publisher=[[Weather.com]]}}</ref>
* The [[Yellowstone Caldera]] is not overdue for a [[supervolcano]] eruption.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|date= May 8, 2015 |title= Five Things Most People Get Wrong About the Yellowstone Volcano (2015) |url=https://www.usgs.gov/volcanoes/yellowstone/five-things-most-people-get-wrong-about-yellowstone-volcano-2015 |publisher=[[Yellowstone Volcano Observatory]] (USGS) |access-date=April 2, 2022}}</ref> There is also no evidence that it will erupt in the near future. In fact, data indicates there will not be an eruption in the coming centuries.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=Modeling the Ash Distribution of a Yellowstone Supereruption (2014) {{!}} U.S. Geological Survey |url=https://www.usgs.gov/volcanoes/yellowstone/modeling-ash-distribution-yellowstone-supereruption-2014 |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=www.usgs.gov}}</ref> The most likely eruption would be [[Hydrothermal explosion|hydrothermal]] rather than volcanic. A [[caldera]]-forming volcanic eruption (and subsequent impacts on global weather patterns and agricultural production) is the least likely scenario and has an extremely low likelihood.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=Questions About Future Volcanic Activity at Yellowstone {{!}} U.S. Geological Survey |url=https://www.usgs.gov/volcanoes/yellowstone/questions-about-future-volcanic-activity-yellowstone |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=www.usgs.gov}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=Could a large Yellowstone eruption significantly change the climate? {{!}} U.S. Geological Survey |url=https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/could-a-large-yellowstone-eruption-significantly-change-climate |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=www.usgs.gov}}</ref>
* The [[Structure of Earth|Earth's interior]] is not molten rock. This misconception may originate from a misunderstanding based on the fact that the [[mantle convection|Earth's mantle convects]], and the incorrect assumption that only liquids and gases can convect. In fact, a solid with a large [[Rayleigh number]] can also convect, given enough time, which is what occurs in the solid mantle due to the very large thermal gradient across it.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|last1=Gupta |first1=H.K. |title=Encyclopedia of Solid Earth Geophysics |date=2011 |publisher=Springer Dordrecht |isbn=978-90-481-8701-0 |page=1539}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|last1=Robertson |first1=E.C. |title=The Interior of the Earth |url=https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/interior/ |publisher=USGS |access-date=July 8, 2022}}</ref> There are small pockets of [[Magma|molten rock]] in the upper mantle, but these make up a tiny fraction of the mantle's volume.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Hata |first1=M. |last2=Uyeshima |first2=M. |title=Temperature and melt fraction distributions in a mantle wedge determined from the electrical conductivity structure: Application to one nonvolcanic and two volcanic regions in the Kyushu subduction zone, Japan |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |date=March 31, 2015 |volume=42 |issue=8 |pages=2709–2717 |doi=10.1002/2015GL063308|bibcode=2015GeoRL..42.2709H |s2cid=128585826}}</ref> The Earth's [[Earth's outer core|outer core]] ''is'' liquid, but it is liquid metal, not rock.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Clement |first1=B.M. |last2=Holzheid |first2=A. |last3=Tilgner |first3=A. |title=Core geophysics |journal=PNAS |date=October 25, 1997 |volume=94 |issue=24 |pages=12742–12743 |doi=10.1073/pnas.94.24.12742|pmid=9370529 |pmc=34384 |bibcode=1997PNAS...9412742C |doi-access=free}}</ref>
* The [[Amazon rainforest]] does not provide 20% of Earth's oxygen. This is a misinterpretation of a 2010 study which found that approximately 34% of photosynthesis by terrestrial plants occurs in tropical rainforests (so the Amazon rainforest would account for approximately half of this). Due to respiration by the resident organisms, all ecosystems (including the Amazon rainforest) have a net output of oxygen of approximately zero. The oxygen currently present in the atmosphere was accumulated over billions of years.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|last=Katarina|first=Zimmer|date=August 28, 2019|title=Why the Amazon doesn't really produce 20% of the world's oxygen |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/environment/article/why-amazon-doesnt-produce-20-percent-worlds-oxygen|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210218183525/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/environment/article/why-amazon-doesnt-produce-20-percent-worlds-oxygen|archive-date=February 18, 2021|access-date=October 8, 2021|website=National Geographic}}</ref>
* [[Bird]] deaths due to [[wind turbine]]s are extremely rare compared to those caused by cats, windows, vehicles, poison, and overhead power lines.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=Threats to Birds / Top Threats to Birds (U.S. only. Ordered by Median Estimate of Bird Mortality Annually. As of 2017.) |url=https://www.fws.gov/library/collections/threats-birds |publisher=U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250213033928/https://www.fws.gov/library/collections/threats-birds |archive-date=13 February 2025 |date=2017 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=How Harmful is Renewable Energy to Birds? {{!}} Article {{!}} EESI |url=https://www.eesi.org/articles/view/how-harmful-is-renewable-energy-to-birds |access-date=2023-06-02 |website=www.eesi.org}}</ref>
* [[File:Contrails.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|Multiple concurrent contrails. How long they last depends upon the weather, especially the temperature, humidity, and wind speed.]] The white streaks seen in the sky after airplanes pass overhead are [[contrails]] consisting of condensed water vapor and engine exhaust. They are not [[Chemtrail conspiracy theory|chemtrails]], nor are they part of a program to control the weather or some other nefarious purpose.<ref name="Quantifying expert consensus">{{cite journal |title=Quantifying expert consensus against the existence of a secret, large-scale atmospheric spraying program|first1=Christine|last1=Shearer|first2=Mick|last2=West|author-link2=Mick West|first3=Ken|last3=Caldeira|first4=Steven J. |last4=Davis |date=1 January 2016 |journal=Environ. Res. Lett.|volume=11|issue=8|article-number=084011|doi=10.1088/1748-9326/11/8/084011|bibcode=2016ERL....11h4011S|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=No, Chemtrails Are Not Real or Causing Floods, E.P.A. Says
 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/10/climate/epa-debunks-chemtrails-conspiracy-theory.html |work=The New York Times |date=July 10, 2025}}</ref>

== Economics ==
[[File:Total population living in extreme poverty, by world region (PovcalNet, World Bank), OWID.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Total population living in extreme poverty, by world region 1987 to 2015<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=Total population living in extreme poverty, by world region |url=https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/total-population-living-in-extreme-poverty-by-world-region |website=Our World in Data |access-date=March 7, 2020}}</ref>]]
* The total number of people living in [[extreme poverty]] globally decreased by two-thirds from 1990 to 2025 (measured using the international poverty line), with other poverty measurements showing similar trends. However, most people surveyed in several countries incorrectly think it has increased or stayed the same.<ref>
* World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform (2025) – processed by Our World in Data. "Number below $3 a day" [dataset]. World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform (2025) [original data].
* {{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Roser |first1=Max |last2=Ortiz-Ospina |first2=Esteban |date=May 25, 2013 |title=Global Extreme Poverty |url=https://ourworldindata.org/extreme-poverty |journal=Our World in Data}}
* {{#invoke:cite|book|last1=Rosling |first1=Hans |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=j-4yDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA7 |title=Factfulness: Ten Reasons We're Wrong About the World{{snd}}and Why Things Are Better Than You Think |last2=Rönnlund |first2=Anna |last3=Rosling |first3=Ola |publisher=Flatiron Books |year=2018 |isbn=978-1-250-12381-7 |page=7}}
* {{#invoke:cite|web|last=Bailey |first=Ronald |date=January 31, 2019 |title=Global Poverty Decline Denialism |url=https://reason.com/2019/01/31/global-poverty-decline-denialism/ |website=[[Reason (magazine)|Reason]]}}</ref> 
* Although the human population of Earth is increasing, the rate of [[Population growth|human population growth]] is decreasing and the world population is expected to peak and then begin falling during the 21st century. Improvements in agricultural productivity and technology are expected to be able to meet anticipated increased demand for resources, making a global [[human overpopulation]] scenario unlikely.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Scudellari|first=Megan|date=December 1, 2015|title=The science myths that will not die|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=528|issue=7582|pages=322–325|doi=10.1038/528322a|pmid=26672537|bibcode=2015Natur.528..322S|s2cid=1414926|issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=Human Overpopulation: Still an Issue of Concern?|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/human-overpopulation-still-an-issue-of-concern/|access-date=October 21, 2021|website=Scientific American|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|last=Piper|first=Kelsey|date=August 20, 2019|title=We've worried about overpopulation for centuries. And we've always been wrong.|url=https://www.vox.com/future-perfect/2019/8/20/20802413/overpopulation-demographic-transition-population-explained|access-date=October 21, 2021|website=Vox|language=en}}</ref>
* For any given [[production set]], there is not a set amount of labor input (a "[[lump of labour fallacy|lump of labor]]") to produce that output. This fallacy is commonly seen in [[Luddite]] and later, related movements as an argument either that automation causes permanent, structural unemployment, or that labor-limiting regulation can decrease unemployment. In fact, changes in capital allocation, efficiency, and [[learning economy|economies of learning]] can change the amount of labor input for a given set of production.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|news|url=http://www.economist.com/economics-a-to-z/l|title=Economics A-Z terms beginning with L|newspaper=The Economist|access-date=December 21, 2016}}
<br/>b. {{cite encyclopedia |last1=Bishop |first1=Matthew |author-link1=Matthew Bishop (journalist) |title=Essential Economics: An A to Z Guide |year=2004 |publisher=Bloomberg Press |isbn=978-1-86197-580-5 |chapter-url=http://www.economist.com/economics-a-to-z/l#node-21529454 |chapter=Lump of labour fallacy |quote=One of the best-known fallacies in ECONOMICS is the notion that there is a fixed amount of work to be done – a lump of LABOUR – which can be shared out in different ways to create fewer or more jobs... |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/essentialeconomi00bish}}</ref>
* Income is not a direct factor in determining [[credit score in the United States]]. Rather, credit score is affected by the amount of unused available credit, which is in turn affected by income.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://okcfox.com/news/consumer-watch/consumer-watch-many-americans-think-income-affects-credit-score|title=Consumer Watch: Many Americans think income affects credit score|first=Mireya|last=Garcia|date=July 15, 2019|website=KOKH}}</ref> Income is also considered when evaluating creditworthiness more generally.
* The US public vastly overestimates the amount spent on [[United States foreign aid#Public opinion|foreign aid]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|last1=DiJulio|first1=Bianca|last2=Norton|first2=Mira|last3=Brodie|first3=Mollyann|date=January 20, 2016|title=Americans' Views on the U.S. Role in Global Health|url=https://www.kff.org/global-health-policy/poll-finding/americans-views-on-the-u-s-role-in-global-health/|access-date=January 12, 2021|website=[[Kaiser Family Foundation]]|language=en-US}}</ref>
* In the US, an increase in [[gross income]] will never reduce a taxpayer's post-tax earnings ([[net income]]) by putting them in a higher [[tax bracket]]. Tax brackets specify [[marginal tax rate|''marginal'' tax rates]]: only income earned in the higher tax bracket is taxed at the higher rate.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.inc.com/mediafeed/lance-cothern/4-myths-about-how-taxes-work-debunked.html|title = 4 Common Misconceptions About Taxes, Debunked |website=Inc. Magazine |last1 = Cothern |first1 = Lance |date = March 25, 2019}}</ref> An increase in gross income can reduce net income in a [[welfare trap]], however, when benefits are withdrawn when passing a certain income threshold.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=Addressing Benefits Cliffs |url=https://www.ncsl.org/research/human-services/addressing-benefits-cliffs.aspx |website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]] |access-date=September 15, 2021 |date=August 20, 2019}}</ref> Prevalence of the misconception varies by political party affiliation.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web| url=https://today.yougov.com/politics/articles/5057-understanding-how-marginal-taxes-work-its-all-part | title=Understanding How Marginal Taxes Work: It's all Party (Yet Again) &#124; YouGov}}</ref>
* Constructing new housing decreases the cost of rent and the price of homes in both the immediate neighborhood and in the city as a whole. In [[real estate economics]], "supply skepticism" leads many Americans to misunderstand the effect of increasing the supply of housing on housing costs. The misconception is unique to the housing market.<ref>{{Cite SSRN |last1=Nall |first1=Clayton |last2=Elmendorf |first2=Christopher |last3=Oklobdzija |first3=Stan |date=15 Nov 2022 |title=Folk Economics and the Persistence of Political Opposition to New Housing |ssrn=4266459}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|last=Levitz |first=Eric |date=2023-08-04 |title=Rent Growth Is Slowing (Where Housing Got Built) |url=https://nymag.com/intelligencer/2023/08/rent-growth-is-slowing-where-housing-got-built.html |access-date=2023-08-04 |website=Intelligencer |language=en-us}}</ref>
* Businesses do not get a tax benefit by [[Checkout charity|collecting charitable donations from their customers]]. Corporation taxes are based on [[profit (accounting)|profit]]; the customer's donation would not change the amount of profit and therefore the tax payable. A business would need to donate ''its own'' money to receive a tax break.<ref name="corptaxusatoday">{{cite news |last=Link |first=Devon |date=2021-06-10 |title=Fact check: Stores cannot use checkout charity funds to offset their own taxes |url=https://eu.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2021/06/10/fact-check-false-claim-checkout-charities-offset-corporate-taxes/7622379002/ |work=[[USA Today]] |access-date=2023-04-01 |archive-date=2021-11-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130110117/https://eu.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2021/06/10/fact-check-false-claim-checkout-charities-offset-corporate-taxes/7622379002/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="corptaxtaxpolicy">{{cite web |url=https://www.taxpolicycenter.org/taxvox/who-gets-tax-benefit-those-checkout-donations-0 |title=Who Gets the Tax Benefit For Those Checkout Donations? |last=Zaretsky |first=Renu |date=2020-11-04 |website=[[Tax Policy Center]] |access-date=2023-04-01 |archive-date=2023-04-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401105956/https://www.taxpolicycenter.org/taxvox/who-gets-tax-benefit-those-checkout-donations-0 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="corptaxap">{{cite news |last=Swenson |first=Ali |date=2021-11-30 |title=Stores can't write off customer donations made at checkout |url=https://apnews.com/article/fact-checking-000329849244 |work=[[Associated Press]] |access-date=2024-11-14 |archive-date=2024-11-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241113063020/https://apnews.com/article/fact-checking-000329849244 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* [[tariff|Import tariffs]] are taxes paid to the government by importers, not by exporting countries or manufacturers as is claimed by some, including [[Donald Trump]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Wiseman |first=Paul |date=2024-09-27 |title=Trump favors huge new tariffs. How do they work? |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/trump-favors-huge-new-tariffs-how-do-they-work |work=[[PBS]] |access-date=2024-12-02 |archive-date=2025-02-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250222003943/https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/trump-favors-huge-new-tariffs-how-do-they-work |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Lotz |first=Avery |date=2024-11-06 |title=Trump's tariffs: How they work, and who would pay |url=https://www.axios.com/2024/09/28/how-tariffs-work-trump-china |work=[[Axios (website)|Axios]] |access-date=2024-12-02 |archive-date=2024-12-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241202232134/https://www.axios.com/2024/09/28/how-tariffs-work-trump-china |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | date=2024-12-13 | title=Most people don't know how tariffs work (and some even admit that) | url=https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/most-people-dont-know-how-tariffs-work-and-some-even-admit | work=[[Ipsos]] | access-date=2025-09-21 | archive-date=2025-09-12 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250912120550/https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/most-people-dont-know-how-tariffs-work-and-some-even-admit | url-status=live}}</ref> There is a near-unanimous consensus among economists that tariffs have a net-negative effect on economic growth and welfare, and harm consumers through higher prices by more than they benefit domestic producers and governments.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Paul R. |last=Krugman |title=The Narrow and Broad Arguments for Free Trade |journal=American Economic Review: Papers and Proceedings |volume=83 |number=3 |date=May 1993 |pages=362–366 |jstor=2117691}}</ref>

== Geography ==
{{See also|Mercator projection#Examples of size distortion}}
[[File:CapeHopeDetail.png|thumb|upright=1.35|The [[Cape of Good Hope]] and [[Cape Agulhas]], the southernmost point of Africa]]
* The [[Cape of Good Hope]] is not the southern tip of Africa; that distinction belongs to [[Cape Agulhas]], located about {{convert|150|km|-1}} to the east-southeast.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.airpano.com/360photo/cape-good-hope-rsa|title=Cape of Good Hope, South Africa. The Most South-Western Point of The African Continent|website=AirPano}}</ref>
* The majority of the [[Sahara]] consists of [[Hamada|rocks]], rather than [[Erg (landform)|sand]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|date=June 19, 2024 |title=Journey through a stunning diversity of cultures and sounds in the Sahara Desert |url=https://www.abc.net.au/listen/programs/passenger/passenger-sahara-cultures-and-sounds/103948632 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240619110922/https://www.abc.net.au/listen/programs/passenger/passenger-sahara-cultures-and-sounds/103948632 |archive-date=June 19, 2024 |access-date=June 20, 2024 |website=[[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]]}}</ref><ref name="sciencedirect.com"/>
* Rivers do not predominantly flow from north to south. [[River#The flow of rivers|Rivers flow downhill]] in all compass directions, often changing direction along their course.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal| url=https://journals.flvc.org/flgeog/article/view/76274 | title=More Than a Few Northerly Running Rivers in the World | journal=The Florida Geographer | date=May 23, 2008 | volume=39 | last1=Kamiar | first1=Mohammad}}</ref><ref name="Rosenberg 2020">{{#invoke:cite|web|last=Rosenberg |first=Matt |date=April 5, 2020 |title=Major Rivers That Flow North |url=https://www.thoughtco.com/rivers-flowing-north-1435099 |access-date=November 8, 2022 |website=ThoughtCo.}}</ref> Many major rivers flow northward, including the [[Nile]], the [[Yenisey]], the [[Ob (river)|Ob]], the [[Rhine]], the [[Lena (river)|Lena]], and the [[Orinoco]].<ref name="Rosenberg 2020"/><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.worldatlas.com/rivers/rivers-that-flow-north.html|title=Rivers That Flow North|date=May 6, 2021}}</ref>

== Human body and health ==
{{See also|Urban legends about drugs|Common misconceptions about birth control}}
[[File:Korean fans closeup.jpg|thumb|[[Fan death|Leaving electric fans on while asleep is not dangerous]].]]

* It is not just [[heavy metals]] which can be toxic; other metals (for example [[beryllium]] and [[lithium]]) can be toxic too.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |year=2024 |entry=Metal Toxicity |title=Dictionary of Toxicology |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/978-981-99-9283-6_1678}}</ref>
* Sleeping in a closed room with an electric fan running does not result in "[[fan death]]", as is widely believed in South Korea among older people.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.esquire.com/news-politics/q-and-a/a5522/korean-fan-death-0209/|title=Why Do Koreans Think Electric Fans Will Kill Them?|date=January 22, 2009|website=Esquire|access-date=August 2, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|news|last=Shapiro |first=Ari |date=August 9, 2015 |title=South Korea's Quirky Notions About Electric Fans |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/parallels/2015/08/09/430341089/south-koreas-quirky-notions-about-electric-fans |access-date=June 15, 2024 |work=[[NPR]]}}</ref> As of 2019, this belief was in decline.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|last=Paolucci |first=Paul |url=https://brill.com/display/title/54437 |title=Acquiring Modernity |chapter=Acquiring Modernity: An Investigation into the Rise, Structure, and Future of the Modern World |publisher=[[Brill Publishers]] |isbn=978-90-04-39395-0 |series=Studies in Critical Social Sciences, Volume: 136 |location=Leiden, The Netherlands |publication-date=July 18, 2019 |page=9}}</ref>
* [[Nocturia]] (waking up at night to urinate) is equally prevalent in women and men,<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=van Kerrebroeck P, Hashim H, Holm-Larsen T, Robinson D, Stanley N |title=Thinking beyond the bladder: antidiuretic treatment of nocturia |journal=Int J Clin Pract |volume=64 |issue=6 |pages=807–16 |date=May 2010 |pmid=20337753 |doi=10.1111/j.1742-1241.2010.02336.x |url=https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl/en/publications/446efd03-0a53-4172-bb7c-6ecb995b72f5}}</ref> although it is more common among those over 50.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nocturia |url=https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/14510-nocturia |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20260620182122/https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/14510-nocturia |archive-date=2026-06-20 |access-date=2026-07-27 |website=Cleveland Clinic |language=en}}</ref>
* [[Sleepwalking#Treatment|Waking up a sleepwalker does not harm them]]. Sleepwalkers may be confused or disoriented for a short time after awakening, but the health risks associated with sleepwalking are from injury or insomnia, not from being awakened.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.medicinenet.com/sleepwalking/article.htm|title=Sleepwalking: Causes, Symptoms, and Treatments|publisher=MedicineNet, Inc| author1=Mersch, John |access-date=May 10, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131026073747/http://www.medicinenet.com/sleepwalking/article.htm |archive-date=October 26, 2013| url-status=live}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.sleepfoundation.org/article/sleep-related-problems/sleepwalking|title=Sleepwalking|publisher=National Sleep Foundation|access-date=May 10, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131229075629/http://www.sleepfoundation.org/article/sleep-related-problems/sleepwalking |archive-date=December 29, 2013| url-status=live}}</ref>
* [[Seizure]]s cannot cause a person to swallow their own tongue,<ref>{{ cite book |vauthors=Tarulli A |year=2021 |chapter=Seizures and Epilepsy |title=Neurology |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-55598-6_20 |isbn=978-3-030-55597-9 |pages=289–315}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Rossi |first1=Kyle C. |last2=Baumgartner |first2=Alexander J. |last3=Goldenholz |first3=Shira R. |last4=Goldenholz |first4=Daniel M. |date=December 2020 |title=Recognizing and refuting the myth of tongue swallowing during a seizure |journal=Seizure |volume=83 |pages=32–37 |doi=10.1016/j.seizure.2020.09.023 |issn=1532-2688 |pmid=33080482|s2cid=222137755 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and it is dangerous to attempt to place a foreign object into a convulsing person's mouth. Instead it is recommended to gently lay a convulsing person on their side to minimize the risk of asphyxiation.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|date=2022-01-03 |title=Seizure First Aid {{!}} Epilepsy {{!}} CDC |url=https://www.cdc.gov/epilepsy/about/first-aid.htm |access-date=2023-11-10 |website=www.cdc.gov |language=en-us}}</ref>
* [[Drowning]] is often inconspicuous to onlookers.<ref name="Vittone">{{#invoke:cite|journal|url=http://www.uscg.mil/hq/cg5/cg534/On%20Scene/OSFall06.pdf |title=It Doesn't Look Like They're Drowning |last=Vittone |first=Mario |page=14 |journal=On Scene: The Journal of U.S. Coast Guard Search and Rescue}}</ref> In most cases, the [[instinctive drowning response]] prevents the victim from waving or yelling,<ref name="Vittone"/> which are therefore not dependable signs of trouble. Most drowning victims do not show prior evidence of distress.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|editor-last1=Fletemeyer|editor-first1=John R. |editor-last2=Freas |editor-first2=Samuel J.|title=Drowning: new perspectives on intervention and prevention |volume=1998|date=1999|page=234|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Xcnwm8zE24QC|last=Pia|first=Frank|chapter=Chapter 14: Reflections on Lifeguard surveillance programs|publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=978-1-57444-223-6}}</ref>
* [[Herbal medicine]]s are not necessarily safe and side-effect free; such medicines can have [[List of herbs with known adverse effects|adverse effects]].<ref>{{cite book |vauthors=Kumar P, Nandave M, Kumar A, Nandave D |year=2024 |chapter= Herbovigilance|veditors=Nandave M, Kumar A |title=Pharmacovigilance Essentials |publisher=Springer | doi=10.1007/978-981-99-8949-2_12 |pages=243–267|isbn=978-981-99-8948-5}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cupp |first=Melanie Johns |date=1999-03-01 |title=Herbal Remedies: Adverse Effects and Drug Interactions |url=https://www.aafp.org/afp/1999/0301/p1239 |journal=American Family Physician |language=en |volume=59 |issue=5 |pages=1239–1244 |pmid=10088878 |issn=1532-0650}}</ref>
* Human blood in [[vein]]s is not actually blue. Blood is red due to the presence of [[hemoglobin]]; deoxygenated blood (in veins) has a deep red color, and oxygenated blood (in [[arteries]]) has a light cherry-red color. Veins below the skin can appear blue or green due to [[subsurface scattering]] of light through the skin, and aspects of human color perception. Many medical diagrams also use blue to show veins, and red to show arteries, which contributes to this misconception.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Kienle|first1=Alwin|first2=Lothar|last2=Lilge|first3=I.Alex|last3=Vitkin|first4=Michael S.|last4=Patterson|first5=Brian C.|last5=Wilson|first6=Raimund|last6=Hibst|first7=Rudolf|last7=Steiner|date=March 1, 1996|title=Why do veins appear blue? A new look at an old question|journal=Applied Optics|volume=35|issue=7|pages=1151–60|url=http://www.imt.liu.se/edu/courses/TBMT36/pdf/blue.pdf|doi=10.1364/AO.35.001151|pmid=21085227|bibcode=1996ApOpt..35.1151K|access-date=April 30, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120210145120/https://www.imt.liu.se/edu/courses/TBMT36/pdf/blue.pdf|archive-date=February 10, 2012}}</ref>
* [[Asystole]], also known as a "flatline", is not a shockable rhythm and is neither treated nor cured via [[defibrillation]]. Medical interventions for asystole include high-quality [[Cardiopulmonary resuscitation|CPR]] and (in a medically professional environment) [[Adrenaline|epinephrine]] administration. The misconception may stem from outdated medical practices and Hollywood glamorization of [[resuscitation]] efforts.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Asystole: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment |url=https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/22920-asystole |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20260723152240/https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/22920-asystole |archive-date=2026-07-23 |access-date=2026-08-25 |website=Cleveland Clinic |language=en}}</ref>
* Exposure to a vacuum, or experiencing all but the most extreme [[uncontrolled decompression]], does not cause the body to explode or internal fluids to boil (although the fluids in the mouth and lungs will indeed boil at altitudes above the [[Armstrong limit]]); rather, it will lead to a loss of [[consciousness]] once the body has depleted the supply of oxygen in the blood, followed by death from [[hypoxia (medical)|hypoxia]] within minutes.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://imagine.gsfc.nasa.gov/ask_astro/space_travel.html|title=Ask an Astrophysicist: How would the unprotected human body react to the vacuum of outer space?|publisher=[[NASA]]|url-status=live|archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/68Aef3glC?url=http://imagine.gsfc.nasa.gov/docs/ask_astro/answers/970603.html|archive-date=June 4, 2012}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.abc.net.au/science/articles/2005/04/07/1320013.htm|title=Exploding Body in Vacuum|work=ABC Science|date=April 6, 2005|url-status=live|archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/68Aef3glC?url=http://imagine.gsfc.nasa.gov/docs/ask_astro/answers/970603.html|archive-date=June 4, 2012}}</ref>
* Exercise-induced [[delayed onset muscle soreness]] is not caused by [[lactic acid]] build-up. Muscular lactic acid levels return to normal levels within an hour after exercise; delayed onset muscle soreness is thought to be due to [[microtrauma]] from unaccustomed or strenuous exercise.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Cheung|first=K|author2=Hume, P |author3=Maxwell, L |title=Delayed onset muscle soreness: treatment strategies and performance factors|journal=Sports Medicine|year=2003|volume=33|issue=2|pages=145–64|pmid=12617692|doi=10.2165/00007256-200333020-00005|s2cid=26525519}}
<br/>b.{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=McHugh |first1=Malachy P. |title=Recent advances in the understanding of the repeated bout effect: the protective effect against muscle damage from a single bout of eccentric exercise |journal=Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports |date=2003 |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=88–97 |issn=0905-7188|pmid=12641640 |doi=10.1034/j.1600-0838.2003.02477.x |s2cid=6697478}}</ref>
* Stretching before or after exercise does not reduce [[delayed onset muscle soreness]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Henschke |first1=Nicholas |last2=Lin |first2=C. Christine |title=Stretching before or after exercise does not reduce delayed-onset muscle soreness |journal=Br J Sports Med |date=December 1, 2011 |volume=45 |issue=15 |pages=1249–50 |doi=10.1136/bjsports-2011-090599 |pmid=22006932 |s2cid=32498886 |url=https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/45/15/1249.full |access-date=September 11, 2018 |language=en |issn=0306-3674}}</ref>
* [[Urine#Bacteria and pathogens|Urine is not sterile]], not even in the bladder.<ref name="Engelhaupt 2014">{{#invoke:cite|news|url=https://www.sciencenews.org/blog/gory-details/urine-not-sterile-and-neither-rest-you|title=Urine is not sterile, and neither is the rest of you|last1=Engelhaupt|first1=Erika|date=May 22, 2014|website=Science News|language=en|access-date=July 31, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180622083801/https://www.sciencenews.org/blog/gory-details/urine-not-sterile-and-neither-rest-you|archive-date=June 22, 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> This misconception may derive from urine bacterial screening tests, which return "negative" when bacteria levels are low, but nonzero.<ref name="Engelhaupt 2014"/>
* Sudden immersion into freezing water does not typically cause death by [[hypothermia]], but rather from the [[cold shock response]], which can cause [[cardiac arrest]], [[heart attack]], or [[hyperventilation]] leading to [[drowning]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Tipton|first1=M. J.|last2=Collier|first2=N.|last3=Massey|first3=H.|last4=Corbett|first4=J.|last5=Harper|first5=M.|date=November 1, 2017|title=Cold water immersion: kill or cure?: Cold water immersion: kill or cure?|journal=Experimental Physiology|language=en|volume=102|issue=11|pages=1335–55|doi=10.1113/EP086283|pmid=28833689|doi-access=free}}</ref>
* [[Cremation|Cremated remains]] are not ashes in the usual sense. After the incineration is completed, the dry bone fragments are swept out of the retort and pulverized by a machine called a ''cremulator'' (essentially a high-capacity, high-speed blender) to process them into "ashes" or "cremated remains".<ref name="green2006">{{#invoke:cite|book|last=Green |first=Jennifer |title=Dealing With Death: Practices and Procedures |author2=Green, Michael |publisher=Jessica Kingsley Publishers |year=2006 |isbn=978-1-84310-381-3 |page=112}}</ref>
* [[File:Alveolus diagram.svg|thumb|The alveoli]] The lung's [[Pulmonary alveolus|alveoli]] are not tiny balloons that expand and contract under positive pressure following the [[Young–Laplace equation]], as is taught in some physiology and medical textbooks. The tissue structure is more like a sponge with polygonal spaces that unfold and fold under negative pressure from the chest wall.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|doi=10.1152/advan.00024.2002 |pmid=12594072 |volume=27 |issue=1 |title=Laplace's Law and the Alveolus: A Misconception of Anatomy and a Misapplication of Physics |journal=Advances in Physiology Education |pages=34–40 |last1=Prange |first1=Henry D. |year=2003|s2cid=7791096}}</ref>
* Half of [[body heat]] is not lost through the head, and covering the head is no more effective at preventing [[Hypothermia|heat loss]] than covering any other portion of the body. Heat is lost from the body in proportion to the amount of exposed skin.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|first6=Joseph|vauthors=Sessler DI, Moayeri A, Støen R, Glosten B, Hynson J, McGuire J|year=1990|title=Thermoregulatory vasoconstriction decreases cutaneous heat loss|journal=Anesthesiology |volume=73|issue=4|pages=656–60|doi=10.1097/00000542-199010000-00011|pmid=2221434|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Gammon 2013">{{#invoke:cite|web|first=Katharine|last=Gammon|date=February 1, 2013|title=Do We Really Lose Half our Body Heat From our Heads?|url=https://www.livescience.com/34411-body-heat-loss-head.html|access-date=January 18, 2022|website=[[Live Science]]|language=en}}</ref> The head accounts for around 7–9% of the body's surface, and studies have shown that having one's head submerged in cold water causes a person to lose only 10% more heat overall.<ref name="Sample 2008">{{cite news |last1=Sample |first1=Ian |date=17 December 2008 |title=Scientists debunk the myth that you lose most heat through your head |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2008/dec/17/medicalresearch-humanbehaviour |access-date=29 July 2024 |work=The Guardian |archive-date=5 September 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130905083755/http://www.theguardian.com/science/2008/dec/17/medicalresearch-humanbehaviour |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Vreeman |first1=Rachel C |last2=Carroll |first2=Aaron E |date=17 December 2008 |title=Festive medical myths |url=https://scholarworks.indianapolis.iu.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/1a1897df-5cf6-451e-ab06-d9127bf0b22a/content |journal=British Medical Journal |volume=337 |article-number=a2769 |doi=10.1136/bmj.a2769 |pmid=19091758 |hdl=1805/4262 }}</ref>
* [[Adrenochrome]] is not harvested from living people and has no use as a recreational drug. [[Hunter S. Thompson]] conceived a fictional drug of the same name in his book ''[[Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas]]'', apparently unaware that a real substance by that name existed; it is Thompson's fictional adrenochrome, and not the real chemical compound, that is the source of numerous conspiracy theories revolving around human trafficking to harvest the fictional drug.<ref name=adams>{{#invoke:cite|news|last1=Adams |first1=Josie |date=April 7, 2020 |title=The truth about adrenochrome |url=https://thespinoff.co.nz/society/07-04-2020/explainer-adrenochrome-the-drug-that-doesnt-exist/ |access-date=June 28, 2020 |work=The Spinoff}}</ref><ref name="friedberg">{{cite magazine |last=Friedberg |first=Brian |title=The Dark Virality of a Hollywood Blood-Harvesting Conspiracy |magazine=Wired |url=https://www.wired.com/story/opinion-the-dark-virality-of-a-hollywood-blood-harvesting-conspiracy/ |access-date=February 21, 2021 |archive-date=August 15, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200815072721/https://www.wired.com/story/opinion-the-dark-virality-of-a-hollywood-blood-harvesting-conspiracy/ |url-status=live}}</ref>
* Men and women have the same number of ribs: 24, or 12 pairs. The erroneous idea that women have one more rib than men may stem from the [[Genesis creation narrative|biblical creation story]] of [[Adam and Eve]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|date=March 12, 2020 |title=How many ribs do humans have? Men, women, and anatomy |first=Danielle |last=Dresden |url=https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/how-many-ribs-do-humans-have#men-vs-women |access-date=June 5, 2022 |website=Medical News Today |language=en |quote=Although many people might think that males have fewer ribs than females — most likely sparked by the biblical story of Adam and Eve — there is no factual evidence.}}</ref>
* The use of [[cotton swab]]s (a.k.a. cotton buds or Q-Tips) in the ear canal has no associated medical benefits and poses definite medical risks.<ref>a. {{citation |last=Moser |first=Rod |url=http://blogs.webmd.com/all-ears/2006/11/q-tips-weapons-of-ear-destruction.html |title=Q-Tips – Weapons of Ear Destruction? |publisher=WebMD |date=13 November 2006 |access-date=26 December 2024 |archive-date=7 October 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101007005456/http://blogs.webmd.com/all-ears/2006/11/q-tips-weapons-of-ear-destruction.html |url-status=live}}
<br/>b. {{citation |first=Joel |last=Stein |url=http://content.time.com/time/nation/article/0,8599,105556,00.html |title=Something Evil in the Ear Canal |magazine=Time |date=26 March 2001 |access-date=26 December 2024 |archive-date=3 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230403230253/https://content.time.com/time/nation/article/0,8599,105556,00.html |url-status=dead}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last=American Academy of Family Physicians|title=Information from Your Family Doctor—Earwax: What You Should Know|journal=American Family Physician|date=May 2007|volume=75|issue=10|page=1530|url=http://www.aafp.org/afp/2007/0515/p1523.html|pmid=17555145}}
<br/>d. {{#invoke:cite|web|url = http://commonhealth.wbur.org/2012/11/q-tips-ears-danger|title = Why You Really, Truly Should Not Put Q-Tips Into Your Ears|website = commonhealth|access-date = 6 March 2016|archive-date = March 3, 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160303043728/http://commonhealth.wbur.org/2012/11/q-tips-ears-danger}}</ref>
* The idea that a precise number of stages of grief exists is not supported in peer-reviewed research or objective clinical observation, let alone the [[five stages of grief]] model.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|news|url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,2042372-2,00.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110131162817/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,2042372-2,00.html|archive-date=January 31, 2011|title=New Ways to Think About Grief|first=Ruth Davis|last=Konigsberg |date=January 29, 2011|access-date=27 November 2016|via=www.time.com}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|journal| vauthors = Corr CA |date=23 October 2018|title=The 'five stages' in coping with dying and bereavement: strengths, weaknesses and some alternatives|journal=Mortality|volume=24|issue=4|pages=405–417|doi=10.1080/13576275.2018.1527826|s2cid=149545381}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|web|last1=Shermer |first1=Michael |title=Five Fallacies of Grief: Debunking Psychological Stages |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/five-fallacies-of-grief/ |website=www.scientificamerican.com |publisher=[[Scientific American]] |date=1 November 2008 |access-date=29 December 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200511014903/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/five-fallacies-of-grief/ |archive-date=11 May 2020}}
<br/>d. {{#invoke:cite|journal| vauthors = Wortman CB, Silver RC |title=The myths of coping with loss | journal = Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology | volume = 57 | issue = 3 | pages = 349–357 | date = June 1989 | pmid = 2661609 | doi = 10.1037/0022-006x.57.3.349}}</ref>
* {{Convert|37|C||sigfig=3}} is not the normal or average [[Human body temperature|temperature of the human body]]. That figure comes from an 1860 study,<ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|url=https://archive.org/details/dasverhaltender00wundgoog|first=Carl Reinhold August|last=Wunderlich|title=Das Verhalten der Eigenwärme in Krankheiten |trans-title=The behavior of the self-warmth in diseases|location=Leipzig|year=1868 <!-- Original print date, per [http://www.uni-leipzig.de/~agintern/uni600/ug174.htm University of Leipzig] -->|publisher=O. Wigand}}; its 1871 2nd edition translated into English and published with the title [https://archive.org/details/ontemperaturein01wundgoog ''On the temperature in diseases: a manual of medical thermometry''].</ref> but modern research shows that the average internal temperature is {{convert|36.4|C}}, with small fluctuations.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|last1=Weintraub |first1=Karen |title=Are Human Body Temperatures Cooling Down? |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/are-human-body-temperatures-cooling-down/ |website=Scientific American |date=April 2020 |access-date=10 March 2022}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal| pmid=1302471 | date=1992 | title=A critical appraisal of 98.6 degrees F, the upper limit of the normal body temperature, and other legacies of Carl Reinhold August Wunderlich | journal=JAMA | volume=268 | issue=12 | pages=1578–1580 | doi=10.1001/jama.1992.03490120092034 | vauthors = MacKowiak PA, Wasserman SS, Levine MM}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web| url=https://www.realclearscience.com/blog/2015/08/the_average_body_temperature_is_not_986_degrees.html | title=The Average Body Temperature is Not 98.6 &#124; RealClearScience | last1=Pomeroy | first1=Ross | work=RealClearScience | date=August 26, 2015}}</ref>
* The [[Human microbiome|cells in the human body]] are not outnumbered 10 to 1 by [[microorganism]]s. The 10 to 1 ratio was an estimate made in 1972; current estimates put the ratio at either 3 to 1 or 1.3 to 1.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|journal| url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature.2016.19136 | doi=10.1038/nature.2016.19136 | title=Scientists bust myth that our bodies have more bacteria than human cells | date=2016 | last1=Abbott | first1=Alison | journal=Nature}}<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|book|last1=Engelhaupt |first1=Erika |title=Gory details: adventures from the dark side of science |title-link=Gory Details |last2=Morrow-Cribbs |first2=Briony |date=2020 |publisher=National geographic partners |isbn=978-1-4262-2097-5 |location=Washington}}<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|web| url=https://www.sciencenews.org/article/bodys-bacteria-dont-outnumber-human-cells-so-much-after-all | title=Body's bacteria don't outnumber human cells so much after all | date=January 8, 2016}}</ref>
* The total length of capillaries in the human body is not 100,000&nbsp;km. That figure comes from a 1929 book by August Krogh, who used an unrealistically large model person and an inaccurately high density of capillaries. The true number is believed to be between 9,000 and 19,000&nbsp;km.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal| pmid=33242636 | date=24 Nov 2020 | title=August Krogh: Muscle capillary function and oxygen delivery | journal=Comp Biochem Physiol A | doi=10.1016/j.cbpa.2020.110852 | vauthors = Poole DC, Kano Y, Koga S, Musch TI | volume=253 | article-number=110852 | pmc=7867635}}</ref>
* Wood smoke, for example from [[wood-burning stoves]], is not a benign form of pollution because it is "natural", but is as harmful as other common forms of air pollution such as [[diesel fumes]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Naeher LP, Brauer M, Lipsett M, Zelikoff JT, Simpson CD, Koenig JQ, Smith KR |title=Woodsmoke health effects: a review |journal=Inhal Toxicol |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=67–106 |date=January 2007 |pmid=17127644 |doi=10.1080/08958370600985875 |bibcode=2007InhTx..19...67N |url=}}</ref>

=== Disease and preventive healthcare ===
{{See also|Misconceptions about HIV and AIDS|COVID-19 misinformation}}

* It is not true that more people have died from the [[COVID-19 vaccine#Adverse events|COVID-19 vaccine]] than from COVID-19 itself.<ref>https://www.kff.org/health-information-and-trust/poll-finding/kff-tracking-poll-on-health-information-and-trust-january-2025/ Four in ten Republicans now say it is "probably" or "definitely true" that "more people have died from COVID-19 vaccines than from the virus itself,"</ref> Severe adverse reactions from the vaccine are rare,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kouhpayeh H, Ansari H |title=Adverse events following COVID-19 vaccination: A systematic review and meta-analysis | journal = International Immunopharmacology | volume = 109 | article-number = 108906 | date = August 2022 | pmid = 35671640 | doi = 10.1016/j.intimp.2022.108906 | pmc = 9148928}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Graña C, Ghosn L, Evrenoglou T, Jarde A, Minozzi S, Bergman H, Buckley BS, Probyn K, Villanueva G, Henschke N, Bonnet H, Assi R, Menon S, Marti M, Devane D, Mallon P, Lelievre JD, Askie LM, Kredo T, Ferrand G, Davidson M, Riveros C, Tovey D, Meerpohl JJ, Grasselli G, Rada G, Hróbjartsson A, Ravaud P, Chaimani A, Boutron I |title=Efficacy and safety of COVID-19 vaccines | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 12 | issue = 12 | article-number = CD015477 | date = December 2022 | pmid = 36473651 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD015477 | pmc = 9726273}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last1=Settles | first1=Gabrielle | url=https://www.poynter.org/fact-checking/2021/claims-that-millions-of-people-have-died-from-the-covid-19-vaccine-are-unfounded/ | title=Claims that millions of people have died from the COVID-19 vaccine are unfounded | work=Poynter | date=5 October 2021}}</ref> and an "exceedingly small" number of deaths have been caused by the vaccine.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://apnews.com/article/fact-check-cdc-covid-vaccine-deaths-910677348223 | title=Posts mischaracterize CDC data on COVID-19 vaccine deaths | website=[[Associated Press News]] | date=11 January 2023}}</ref> Meanwhile, the death toll from the disease itself is in the millions.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.who.int/data/stories/the-true-death-toll-of-covid-19-estimating-global-excess-mortality | title=The true death toll of COVID-19 estimating global excess mortality}}</ref>
* [[Tuberculosis]] is not purely a disease of the lungs that has symptoms of coughing. It may instead infect a wide range of other organs in the body.<ref>{{cite book |vauthors=Kamboj A, Lause M, Kamboj K |year=2023 |chapter=The Problem of Tuberculosis: Myths, Stigma, and Mimics |veditors=Rezaei N |title=Tuberculosis |series=Integrated Science |volume=11 |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-15955-8_50 |pages=1046–1062 |isbn=978-3-031-15954-1}}</ref>
* Cancer cannot be treated by restricting food intake and so supposedly "starving" tumors. Rather, the health of people with cancer is best served by maintaining a [[healthy diet]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Grimes DR, O'Riordan E |title=Starving cancer and other dangerous dietary misconceptions |journal=Lancet Oncol |volume=24 |issue=11 |pages=1177–1178 |date=November 2023 |pmid=37922928 |doi=10.1016/S1470-2045(23)00483-7 |url=}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-30 |title=Diets, Supplements, and Cancer - NCI |url=https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/cam/diets-supplements |access-date=2026-07-25 |website=www.cancer.gov |language=en}}</ref>
* The [[Common cold#Weather|common cold]] and the [[common flu]] are caused by [[virus]]es, not exposure to cold temperatures. However, low temperatures may somewhat weaken the immune system, and someone already infected with a cold or influenza virus but showing no symptoms can become symptomatic after they are exposed to low temperatures.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|title=Temperature-dependent innate defense against the common cold virus limits viral replication at warm temperature in mouse airway cells |year=2015 |pmc=4311828 |last1=Foxman |first1=E. F. |last2=Storer |first2=J. A. |last3=Fitzgerald |first3=M. E. |last4=Wasik |first4=B. R. |last5=Hou |first5=L. |last6=Zhao |first6=H. |last7=Turner |first7=P. E. |last8=Pyle |first8=A. M. |last9=Iwasaki |first9=A. |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=112 |issue=3 |pages=827–832 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1411030112 |pmid=25561542 |bibcode=2015PNAS..112..827F |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Mourtzoukou">{{#invoke:cite|journal| vauthors = Mourtzoukou EG, Falagas ME |title=Exposure to cold and respiratory tract infections | journal = The International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease | volume = 11 | issue = 9 | pages = 938–43 | date = September 2007 | pmid = 17705968}}</ref> Viruses are more likely to spread during the winter for a variety of reasons such as dry air, less air circulation in homes, people spending more time indoors, and lower [[vitamin D]] levels in humans.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|journal|doi = 10.1177/1090198111407187|pmid = 21586668|title = Age and Ethnic Differences in Cold Weather and Contagion Theories of Colds and Flu|journal = Health Education & Behavior|volume = 39|issue = 1|pages = 67–76 |year = 2012|last1 = Sigelman|first1 = Carol K.|s2cid = 206684728}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|journal| pmc=1011011 | pmid=6364570 | volume=139 | issue=6 | title=Traditional health beliefs and practices among lower class black Americans | year=1983 | author=Snow LF | journal=West J Med | pages=820–28}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|journal| pmc=1011011 | pmid=6364570 | volume=139 | title=Traditional health beliefs and practices among lower class black Americans | year=1983 | author=Snow LF | journal=West J Med | issue=6 | pages=820–28}}
<br/>d. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://theconversation.com/mondays-medical-myth-you-can-catch-a-cold-by-getting-cold-2488|title=Monday's medical myth: you can catch a cold by getting cold|first=Merlin|last=Thomas|website=The Conversation|date=July 25, 2011}}
<br/>e. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://blogs.unimelb.edu.au/sciencecommunication/2017/08/17/feeling-cold-causing-colds/|title=Feeling cold causing colds? – Scientific Scribbles}}
<br/>f. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://well.blogs.nytimes.com/2009/06/29/11-health-myths-that-may-surprise-you/|archive-url=https://archive.today/20190418031550/https://well.blogs.nytimes.com/2009/06/29/11-health-myths-that-may-surprise-you/?mtrref=www.google.com&gwh=930ECABDD5CB84FF9CAB5CCC66B35FE7&gwt=pay|title=11 Health Myths That May Surprise You|first=Tara|last=Parker-Pope|date=June 29, 2009|archive-date = April 18, 2019}}

<br/>g. {{#invoke:cite|web|date=December 6, 2021 |title=Winter Illness Guide |url=https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/conditions-and-diseases/winter-illness-guide |access-date=June 21, 2022 |website=www.hopkinsmedicine.org |language=en}}

<br/>h. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Acharya |first1=B. |last2=Thapa |first2=K. |date=January 2016 |title=Indoor Staying During Winter Season Makes People More Susceptible to Flu |journal=[[Journal of Nepal Health Research Council]] |volume=14 |issue=32 |pages=69–70 |issn=1999-6217 |pmid=27426715}}</ref>
* [[Antibiotics]] will not cure a cold; they treat bacterial diseases and are ineffectual against viruses.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/antibiotic-use/colds.html|title=Suffering from a cold?|work=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention |date=October 6, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|url=https://www.fda.gov/drugs/resources-you-drugs/warning-antibiotics-dont-work-viruses-colds-and-flu|title = WARNING: Antibiotics don't work for viruses like colds and the flu|journal = FDA|date = November 3, 2018}}</ref> However, they are sometimes prescribed to prevent or treat [[opportunistic infection|secondary infections]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Arroll |first1=B |last2=Kenealy |first2=T |title=Antibiotics for the common cold and acute purulent rhinitis |journal=The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |date=October 21, 2002 |issue=3 |article-number=CD000247 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD000247 |pmid=12137610}}</ref>
* There is little to no evidence that any illnesses are curable through [[essential oil]]s or [[aromatherapy]],<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Lee|first1=Myeong Soo|last2=Choi|first2=Jiae Choi|title=Aromatherapy for health care: an overview of systematic reviews|journal=Maturitas|date=2012|volume=3|issue=71|pages=257–260|doi=10.1016/j.maturitas.2011.12.018|pmid=22285469}}</ref> and [[Fish oil (medical use)|fish oil]] has not been shown to cure [[dementia]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/do-essential-oils-work-heres-what-science-says/|title=Do Essential Oils Work? Here's What Science Says|publisher=Scientific American|date=March 7, 2020}}</ref>
* In those with the common cold, the color of the [[sputum]] or nasal secretion may vary from colorless to yellow to green and does not indicate the class of agent causing the infection.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|book|editor-first=Ronald |editor-last=Eccles |editor2-first=Olaf |editor2-last=Weber|title=Common cold|page=7|date=2009|publisher=Birkhäuser|location=Basel|isbn=978-3-7643-9894-1}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|book|last=Rutter|first=Paul|title=Community pharmacy: symptoms, diagnosis and treatment|date=2009|publisher=Elsevier/Churchill Livingstone|location=Edinburgh|isbn=978-0-7020-2995-0|page=7|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5nYPvgAACAAJ|edition=2nd}}</ref> The color of the sputum is determined by [[White blood cell|immune cells]] fighting an infection in the nasal area.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Davis |first=Daniel M. |date=2021-11-05 |title=Immunology meets the masses|journal=Science |volume=374 |issue=6568 |page=697 |doi=10.1126/science.abm0134 |pmid=34735237 |bibcode=2021Sci...374..697D |s2cid=243761609 |issn=0036-8075}}</ref>
* [[Vitamin C]] [[Vitamin C and the common cold|does not prevent or treat]] the common cold, although it may have a protective effect during intense cold-weather exercise. If taken daily, it may slightly reduce the duration and severity of colds, but it has no effect if taken after the cold starts.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.webmd.com/cold-and-flu/cold-guide/vitamin-c-for-common-cold |title=Vitamin C for the Common Cold |website=WebMD |access-date=September 27, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101024044649/http://www.webmd.com/cold-and-flu/cold-guide/vitamin-c-for-common-cold |archive-date=October 24, 2010 |url-status=live}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|journal|title=Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold |author=Harri Hemilä |author2=Elizabeth Chalker |journal=[[The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews]] |date=Jan 2013 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD000980.pub4 |pmid=23440782 |volume=1 |issue=1 |article-number=CD000980 |pmc=1160577}}</ref>
* Supplements of the plant [[echinacea]] do not prevent or reduce the severity of colds as widely believed. A 2014 review of 24 different randomized controlled trials found echinacea supplements do not prevent colds, with most showing no benefit over placebo.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schoop |first1=Roland |last2=Klein |first2=Peter |last3=Suter |first3=Andy |last4=Johnston |first4=Bradley C. |title=Echinacea in the prevention of the common cold |journal=Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |year=2014 |issue=2 |article-number=CD000530 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD000530.pub3 |pmid=24554461 |pmc=4068831 }} The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health states there is insufficient evidence to confirm Echinacea's effectiveness for cold prevention or treatment.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/echinacea |title=Echinacea |publisher=National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health |date=2020-08-01 |access-date=2025-10-15}} Variability in product composition (e.g., species, preparation, dosage) and study quality contributes to inconsistent results.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barrett |first1=Bruce |last2=Brown |first2=Roger |last3=Rakel |first3=David |title=Echinacea for Treating the Common Cold: A Randomized Trial |journal=Annals of Internal Medicine |year=2010 |volume=153 |issue=12 |pages=769–777 |doi=10.7326/0003-4819-153-12-201012210-00003 |pmid=21173411 |pmc=3056276}} This misconception is propagated by supplement manufacturers, wellness media, and some health blogs that overstate Echinacea's benefits without acknowledging the limited scientific support.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.health.harvard.edu/staying-healthy/can-supplements-help-your-immunity |title=Can supplements help your immunity? |publisher=Harvard Health Publishing |date=2021-01-25 |access-date=2025-10-15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.webmd.com/cold-and-flu/echinacea-common-cold |title=Echinacea and the Common Cold |publisher=WebMD |date=2023-03-15 |access-date=2025-10-15}}</ref>
* [[File:Bombina bombina 1 (Marek Szczepanek).jpg|thumb|alt=A toad.|The bumps on a toad are not [[wart]]s and cannot cause warts on humans.]] Humans cannot catch warts from toads or other animals; the bumps on a toad are not warts.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.webmd.com/skin-problems-and-treatments/warts-faq-questions-answers#1 | title=Warts: 10 Answers to Common Questions| work=WebMD}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.londondrugs.com/Cultures/en-US/FocusOnHealth/Fall2002/Warts.htm|title=Putting an End to Warts|publisher=Londondrugs.com|access-date=August 29, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120609023506/http://www.londondrugs.com/Cultures/en-US/FocusOnHealth/Fall2002/Warts.htm |archive-date=June 9, 2012| url-status=live}}</ref> [[Wart]]s on human skin are caused by [[human papillomavirus]], which is known to affect only humans.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=Pink Book (Human Papillomavirus) |url=https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/pubs/pinkbook/downloads/hpv.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170321110050/https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/pubs/pinkbook/downloads/hpv.pdf |archive-date=21 March 2017 |access-date=18 April 2017 |website=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]]}}</ref>
* [[cracking joints|Cracking one's knuckles]] does not cause [[osteoarthritis]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Rizvi|first1=Asad|last2=Loukas|first2=Marios|last3=Oskouian|first3=Rod J.|last4=Tubbs|first4=R.
