There is not a shred of evidence to back up either claim, and every reason to assume they are both false. Yet both claims, along with various others in a similar vein, live on.}}</ref>
* The repeating decimal written as [[0.999...]] represents exactly the same quantity as [[1 (number)|1]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|first=John |last=Stillwell |author-link=John Stillwell |title=Elements of algebra: geometry, numbers, equations|year=1994|publisher=Springer |page=42}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|last=Bunch |first=Bryan H. |title=Mathematical fallacies and paradoxes |year=1982 |publisher=Van Nostrand Reinhold |isbn=978-0-442-24905-2|page=119}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Tall|first1=David|author-link1=David Tall |last2=Schwarzenberger|first2=R. L. E.|author-link2=Rolph Ludwig Edward Schwarzenberger |title=Conflicts in the Learning of Real Numbers and Limits|journal=Mathematics Teaching|year=1978|volume=82|pages=6, 44–49|url=http://www.warwick.ac.uk/staff/David.Tall/pdfs/dot1978c-with-rolph.pdf |access-date=May 3, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090530043040/http://www.warwick.ac.uk/staff/David.Tall/pdfs/dot1978c-with-rolph.pdf| archive-date=May 30, 2009}}</ref>
* The [[p-value|''p''-value]] is not the probability that the [[null hypothesis]] is true, or the probability that the [[alternative hypothesis]] is false; it is the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as the results actually observed under the assumption that the null hypothesis was correct, which can indicate the incompatibility of results with the specific statistical model assumed in the null hypothesis.<ref name="asa2016">{{#invoke:cite|journal|vauthors=Wasserstein RL, Lazar NA |year=2016 |title=The ASA's statement on ''p''-values: context, process, and purpose |journal=[[The American Statistician]] |volume=70 |issue=2 |pages=129–33 |doi=10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108|s2cid=124084622 |url=https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/Real_World/ASA_statement.pdf |doi-access=free}}</ref> This misconception, and similar ones like it, contributes to the common [[misuse of p-values|misuse of ''p''-values]] in education and research.<ref name="asa2016"/><ref name="Sterne2001">{{#invoke:cite|journal| vauthors = Sterne JA, Davey Smith G |title=Sifting the evidence-what's wrong with significance tests? | journal = BMJ | volume = 322 | issue = 7280 | pages = 226–31 | date = January 2001 | pmid = 11159626 | pmc = 1119478 | doi = 10.1136/bmj.322.7280.226}}</ref>
* If one were to flip a [[fair coin]] five times and get heads each time, it would not be any more likely for a sixth flip to come up tails. Phrased another way, after a long and/or unlikely [[wikt:streak#:~:text=A continuous series of like events|streak]] of [[Independence (probability theory)|independently]] [[random]] events, the probability of the next event is not influenced by the preceding events. [[Gambler's fallacy|Humans often feel that the underrepresented outcome is more likely]], as if it is due to happen. Such thinking may be attributed to the mistaken belief that gambling, or even chance itself, is a fair process that can correct itself in the event of streaks.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|journal|author=J. Michael Shaughnessy |year=1977 |title=Misconceptions of probability: An experiment with a small-group, activity-based, model building approach to introductory probability at the college level |journal=Educational Studies in Mathematics |volume=8 |issue=3 |pages=295–316 |doi=10.1007/BF00385927|s2cid=120555285}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|book|author=Henk&nbsp;Tijms |title=Understanding Probability: Chance Rules in Everyday Life |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-521-70172-3 |page=79}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|book|author=Maxwell, Nicholas |title=Data Matters: Conceptual Statistics for a Random World |publisher=Key College |year=2004 |isbn=1-930190-89-1 |page=63}}
<br/>d. {{#invoke:cite|book|title=The Corsini Encyclopedia of Psychology and Behavioral Science |publisher=Wiley |year=2000 |isbn=0-471-24097-4 |editor=W.&nbsp;Edward&nbsp;Craighead, Charles&nbsp;B.&nbsp;Nemeroff |volume=2 |page=617}}
<br/>e. Oppenheimer, D.M., & Monin, B. (2009). The retrospective gambler's fallacy: Unlikely events, constructing the past, and multiple universes. ''Judgment and Decision Making, vol. 4, no. 5,'' pp. 326-334
<br/>f. {{#invoke:cite|web|date=2015-01-02 |title=Why we gamble like monkeys |url=http://www.bbc.com/future/story/20150127-why-we-gamble-like-monkeys |work=BBC.com}}
<br/>g. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Rogers |first1=Paul |year=1998 |title=The cognitive psychology of lottery gambling: A theoretical review |journal=Journal of Gambling Studies |volume=14 |issue=2 |pages=111–134 |doi=10.1023/A:1023042708217 |issn=1050-5350 |pmid=12766438 |s2cid=21141130}}</ref>

== Physics ==
[[File:Equal transit-time NASA wrong1.gif|thumb|right|upright=1.35|An illustration of the ''incorrect'' equal transit-time explanation of airfoil lift]]
* The [[Lift (force)|lift force]] is not generated by the air taking the same time to travel above and below an aircraft's wing.<ref name="NASA_Incorrect_Theory1">{{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.grc.nasa.gov/WWW/K-12/airplane/wrong1.html |title=Incorrect Lift Theory |publisher=NASA Glenn Research Center |work=grc.nasa.gov |date=July 28, 2008 |access-date=January 13, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140427084226/http://www.grc.nasa.gov/WWW/K-12/airplane/wrong1.html |archive-date=April 27, 2014}} (Java applet).</ref> This misconception, sometimes called the [[equal transit-time fallacy]], is widespread among textbooks and non-technical reference books, and even appears in pilot training materials. In fact, the air moving over the top of an aerofoil generating lift is always moving much faster than the equal transit theory would imply,<ref name="NASA_Incorrect_Theory1"/> as described in the [[Equal transit-time fallacy|incorrect]] and [[Lift (force)#Simplified physical explanations of lift on an airfoil|correct explanations]] of lift force.

[[File:Blowing over and under a piece of paper.jpg|thumb|Blowing over a piece of paper causes it to rise. Blowing under a piece of paper also causes it to rise. Neither is a demonstration of Bernoulli's Principle.<ref name="Craig">{{cite web| quote= If the lift in figure A were caused by "Bernoulli's principle," then the paper in figure B should droop further when air is blown beneath it. However, as shown, it raises when the upward pressure gradient in downward-curving flow adds to atmospheric pressure at the paper lower surface. |first=Gale M. |last=Craig |title=Physical Principles of Winged Flight |url= http://www.rcgroups.com/forums/showatt.php?attachmentid=5305482 |access-date=March 31, 2016 | via= rcgroups.com}}</ref>]]
* Blowing over a curved piece of paper does not demonstrate [[Bernoulli's principle#Misconceptions and misapplications|Bernoulli's principle]]. Although a common classroom experiment is often explained this way,<ref>a. {{cite magazine |title=This occurs because of Bernoulli's principle – fast-moving air has lower pressure than non-moving air |url=http://makeprojects.com/Project/Origami-Flying-Disk/327/1 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130103152803/http://makeprojects.com/Project/Origami-Flying-Disk/327/1%23.UOWjZ33LdRw |archive-date=January 3, 2013 |access-date=September 5, 2012 |magazine=Make Magazine}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|title=Paper Lift |url=https://physicsforce.umn.edu/content/paper-lift-0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112021453/https://physicsforce.umn.edu/content/paper-lift-0 |archive-date=November 12, 2020 |access-date=January 7, 2021 |work=Physics Force |publisher=University of Minnesota}}.
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|web|title=Educational Packet |url=http://www.tallshipschannelislands.com/PDFs/Educational_Packet.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203014334/http://www.tallshipschannelislands.com/PDFs/Educational_Packet.pdf |archive-date=December 3, 2013 |access-date=June 25, 2012 |work=Tall Ships Festival: Channel Islands Harbor |url-status=usurped |quote=Bernoulli's Principle states that faster moving air has lower pressure... You can demonstrate Bernoulli's Principle by blowing over a piece of paper held horizontally across your lips."}}</ref> Bernoulli's principle applies only within a flow field, and the air above and below the paper are in different flow fields.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|web|last=Craig |first=Gale M. |title=Physical Principles of Winged Flight |url=http://www.regenpress.com/aerodynamics.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210307172349/http://regenpress.com/aerodynamics.pdf |archive-date=March 7, 2021 |access-date=September 5, 2012 |quote=If the lift in figure A were caused by "Bernoulli principle," then the paper in figure B should droop further when air is blown beneath it. However, as shown, it raises when the upward pressure gradient in downward-curving flow adds to atmospheric pressure at the paper lower surface.}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Babinsky |first=Holger |year=2003 |title=How Do Wings Work |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/230910482 |journal=Physics Education |volume=38 |pages=497–502 |bibcode=2003PhyEd..38..497B |doi=10.1088/0031-9120/38/6/001 |s2cid=1657792 |access-date=January 7, 2021 |number=6}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Eastwell |first=Peter |year=2007 |title=Bernoulli? Perhaps, but What About Viscosity? |url=http://d1vdx9ifs4n5d7.cloudfront.net/s3fs-public/davidson_images/eastwell-bernoulli.pdf |journal=The Science Education Review |volume=6 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180318183632/http://d1vdx9ifs4n5d7.cloudfront.net/s3fs-public/davidson_images/eastwell-bernoulli.pdf |archive-date=March 18, 2018 |access-date=September 10, 2023 |quote=...air does not have a reduced lateral pressure (or static pressure...) simply because it is caused to move, the static pressure of free air does not decrease as the speed of the air increases, it misunderstanding Bernoulli's principle to suggest that this is what it tells us, and the behavior of the curved paper is explained by other reasoning than Bernoulli's principle. ... An explanation based on Bernoulli's principle is not applicable to this situation, because this principle has nothing to say about the interaction of air masses having different speeds... Also, while Bernoulli's principle allows us to compare fluid speeds and pressures along a single streamline and... along two different streamlines that originate under identical fluid conditions, using Bernoulli's principle to compare the air above and below the curved paper in Figure 1 is nonsensical; in this case, there aren't any streamlines at all below the paper!}}
<br/>d. {{#invoke:cite|web|last=Raskin |first=Jef |title=Coanda Effect: Understanding Why Wings Work |url=http://karmak.org/archive/2003/02/coanda_effect.html}}
<br/>e. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Auerbach |first=David |year=2000 |title=Why Aircraft Fly |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/230994575 |journal=European Journal of Physics |volume=21 |issue=4 |pages=292, 295 |bibcode=2000EJPh...21..289A |doi=10.1088/0143-0807/21/4/302 |s2cid=250821727}}
<br/>f. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Smith |first1=Norman F. |date=November 1972 |title=Bernoulli and Newton in Fluid Mechanics |journal=The Physics Teacher |volume=10 |issue=8 |pages=451–455 |bibcode=1972PhTea..10..451S |doi=10.1119/1.2352317}}</ref> The paper rises because the air follows the curve of the paper and a curved [[Streamlines, streaklines, and pathlines|streamline]] will develop pressure differences perpendicular to the airflow.<ref name="airflow">a. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Babinsky |first=Holger |year=2003 |title=How Do Wings Work |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/230910482 |journal=Physics Education |volume=38 |issue=6 |pages=497–503 |bibcode=2003PhyEd..38..497B |doi=10.1088/0031-9120/38/6/001 |s2cid=1657792 |access-date=January 7, 2021 |quote=...if a streamline is curved, there must be a pressure gradient across the streamline, with the pressure increasing in the direction away from the centre of curvature.}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Smith |first1=Norman F. |date=April 1973 |title=Bernoulli, Newton, and Dynamic Lift Part II*: Bernoulli or Newton? |journal=School Science and Mathematics |volume=73 |issue=4 |pages=327–335 |doi=10.1111/j.1949-8594.1973.tb09040.x |quote=The curved paper turns the stream of air downward, and this action produces the lift reaction that lifts the paper.}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|web|title=AERONAUTICS: An Educator's Guide with Activities in Science, Mathematics, and Technology Education |url=http://www.nasa.gov/pdf/58152main_Aeronautics.Educator.pdf |access-date=January 7, 2021 |publisher=NASA |page=26 |quote=The curved surface of the tongue creates unequal air pressure and a lifting action. ... Lift is caused by air moving over a curved surface.}}</ref><ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|book|last1=Anderson |first1=David F. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=52Hfn7uEGSoC&pg=PA229 |title=Understanding Flight |last2=Eberhardt |first2=Scott |publisher=McGraw Hill Professional |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-07-138666-1 |page=229 |quote=Demonstrations" of Bernoulli's principle are often given as demonstrations of the physics of lift. They are truly demonstrations of lift, but certainly not of Bernoulli's principle. |via=Google Books}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|book|last=Feil |first=Max |title=The Aeronautics File |quote=As an example, take the misleading experiment most often used to "demonstrate" Bernoulli's principle. Hold a piece of paper so that it curves over your finger, then blow across the top. The paper will rise. However most people do not realize that the paper would NOT rise if it was flat, even though you are blowing air across the top of it at a furious rate. Bernoulli's principle does not apply directly in this case. This is because the air on the two sides of the paper did not start out from the same source. The air on the bottom is ambient air from the room, but the air on the top came from your mouth where you actually increased its speed without decreasing its pressure by forcing it out of your mouth. As a result the air on both sides of the flat paper actually has the same pressure, even though the air on the top is moving faster. The reason that a curved piece of paper does rise is that the air from your mouth speeds up even more as it follows the curve of the paper, which in turn lowers the pressure according to Bernoulli.}}</ref>
* The [[Coriolis effect]] does not cause water to consistently drain from basins in a clockwise/counter-clockwise direction depending on the hemisphere. The common myth often refers to the draining action of flush toilets and bathtubs. In fact, rotation is determined by whatever minor rotation is initially present at the time the water starts to drain, as the magnitude of the Coriolis acceleration is [[rossby number|negligibly small]] compared to the inertial acceleration of flow within a typical basin.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|web|title=Bad Coriolis |url=http://www.ems.psu.edu/~fraser/Bad/BadCoriolis.html |access-date=2016-12-21 |work=www.ems.psu.edu}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|date=April 28, 2003 |title=Flush Bosh |url=http://www.snopes.com/science/coriolis.asp |access-date=2016-12-21 |work=[[Snopes]]}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|web|date=2009-07-20 |title=Does the rotation of the Earth affect toilets and baseball games? |url=http://science.howstuffworks.com/science-vs-myth/everyday-myths/rotation-earth-toilet-baseball2.htm |access-date=2016-12-21}}
<br/>d. {{#invoke:cite|web|title=Can somebody finally settle this question: Does water flowing down a drain spin in different directions depending on which hemisphere you're in? And if so, why? |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/can-somebody-finally-sett/ |access-date=2016-12-21 |work=www.scientificamerican.com}}
<br/>e. {{#invoke:cite|book|author1=Larry D. Kirkpatrick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8hOLs-bmiYYC&pg=PA168 |title=Physics: A World View |author2=Gregory E. Francis |publisher=Cengage Learning |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-495-01088-3 |pages=168–9}}
<br/>f. {{#invoke:cite|journal|author1=Y. A. Stepanyants |author2=G. H. Yeoh |year=2008 |title=Stationary bathtub vortices and a critical regime of liquid discharge |url=http://eprints.usq.edu.au/5726/2/Stepanyants_Yeoh_2008_PV.pdf |journal=Journal of Fluid Mechanics |volume=604 |issue=1 |pages=77–98 |bibcode=2008JFM...604...77S |doi=10.1017/S0022112008001080 |s2cid=53071268 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220723091453/https://eprints.usq.edu.au/5726/2/Stepanyants_Yeoh_2008_PV.pdf |archive-date=July 23, 2022 |access-date=July 23, 2022}}
<br/>g. {{#invoke:cite|book|author=Creative Media Applications |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fF0TTZVQuZoC&pg=PA22 |title=A Student's Guide to Earth Science: Words and terms |publisher=Greenwood Publishing Group |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-313-32902-9 |page=22}}</ref>
* [[General relativity]] does not imply that mass increases as an object approaches the [[speed of light]]; it is an object's [[momentum]], a quantity dependent upon both mass and velocity, that increases [[Asymptote|asymptotically]] as it approaches the speed of light. The mass-energy equivalence equation is thus more accurately expressed as E=γmc², where γ is a variable dependent upon velocity. For an object at rest, γ=1 resulting in the familiar equation E=mc².<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lincoln |first=Don |date=2025-08-29 |title=Mass misconception: The real reason we can't outpace light speed |url=https://bigthink.com/hard-science/light-speed-relativistic-mass/ |access-date=2025-08-31 |website=Big Think |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Halliday = |first = David |date = 1988|title =Fundamentals of Physics Third Edition |url = https://drive.google.com/file/d/12WxyaSNk9NHy_UVS1dFyBu1pPtqebHxB/view |location = |publisher =John Wiley and Sons, Inc. |page = 967 |isbn =0-471-81995-6}}</ref>
* Neither [[Bicycle and motorcycle dynamics#Gyroscopic effects|gyroscopic forces]] nor [[Trail (steering)|geometric trail]] are required for a rider to [[bicycle and motorcycle dynamics#Other hypotheses|balance]] a bicycle or for it to demonstrate [[Bicycle and motorcycle dynamics#Self-stability|self-stability]].<ref name="KMPRS">{{#invoke:cite|journal|journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |author=J. D. G. Kooijman |author2=J. P. Meijaard |author3=J. M. Papadopoulos| author4=A. Ruina |author5=A. L. Schwab |date=April 15, 2011 |title=A bicycle can be self-stable without gyroscopic or caster effects |volume=332 |issue=6027 |pages=339–342 |doi=10.1126/science.1201959 |pmid=21493856 |bibcode=2011Sci...332..339K |s2cid=12296078 |url=http://bicycle.tudelft.nl/stablebicycle/StableBicyclev34Revised.pdf |access-date=January 22, 2013}}</ref><ref name="BikeGyro">a. {{#invoke:cite|book|title=Bicycling Science|edition=2nd|last1=Whitt|first1=Frank R.|first2=David G.|last2=Wilson|date=1982|publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology|isbn=978-0-262-23111-4|pages=198–233}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|last=Klein |first=Richard E. |display-authors=etal |title=Bicycle Science |url=http://www.losethetrainingwheels.org/default.aspx?Lev=2&ID=34 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061010070125/http://www.losethetrainingwheels.org/default.aspx?Lev=2&ID=34 |archive-date=October 10, 2006 |access-date=August 4, 2006 |publisher=LoseTheTrainingWheels.org}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Jones |first1=David E. H. |date=1970 |title=The Stability of the Bicycle |url=http://socrates.berkeley.edu/%7Efajans/Teaching/MoreBikeFiles/JonesBikeBW.pdf |journal=Physics Today |volume=23 |issue=4 |pages=34–40 |bibcode=1970PhT....23d..34J |doi=10.1063/1.3022064}}</ref> Although gyroscopic forces and trail can be contributing factors, it [[Two-mass-skate bicycle|has been demonstrated]] that those factors are neither required nor sufficient by themselves.<ref name="KMPRS"/>
* A penny dropped from the [[Empire State Building]] would not kill a person or crack the sidewalk. A penny is too light and has too much air resistance to acquire enough speed to do much damage since it reaches [[terminal velocity]] after falling about {{convert|50|ft|0|disp=flip}}. Heavier or more aerodynamic objects could cause significant damage if dropped from that height.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=Could a Penny Dropped off a Skyscraper Actually Kill You? |author=Wolchover, Natalie|date=March 5, 2012|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/could-a-penny-dropped-off/ |website=[[Scientific American]]}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=What would happen if you were hit by a penny falling from a skyscraper?|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation-now/2017/03/15/what-would-happen-if-you-were-hit-penny-falling-skyscraper/99160982/|website=[[USA Today]]}}</ref>
* Using a [[programmable thermostat]]'s setback feature to limit heating or cooling in a temporarily unoccupied building does not waste as much energy as leaving the temperature constant. Using setback saves energy (5–15%) because [[heat transfer]] across the surface of the building is roughly proportional to the temperature difference between its inside and the outside.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=Thermostats|website=Energy.gov |url=https://www.energy.gov/energysaver/thermostats}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.achrnews.com/articles/98114-programmable-thermostat-myths-know-the-facts-and-boost-your-profits|title=Programmable thermostat myths: Know the facts and boost your profits|website=www.achrnews.com}}</ref>
* It is not possible for a person to completely submerge in quicksand, as commonly depicted in fiction,<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=Quicksand myth exposed|author=Patricia Reaney|date=September 29, 2005|agency=Reuters |url=https://www.abc.net.au/science/articles/2005/09/29/1471116.htm|website=www.abc.net.au|language=en-AU|access-date=April 8, 2020}}</ref> although sand entrapment in the nearshore of a body of water can be a drowning hazard as the tide rises.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20160323-can-quicksand-really-suck-you-to-your-death|title=Can quicksand really suck you to your death?|last=Hammond|first=Claudia|website=www.bbc.com|date=29 March 2016 |language=en|access-date=April 8, 2020}}</ref>
* [[Quantum nonlocality]] caused by [[quantum entanglement]] does not allow [[faster-than-light communication]] or imply instant [[action at a distance]], despite its common characterization as "spooky action at a distance". Rather, it means that [[Bell test|certain experiments]] cannot be explained by [[local realism]].<ref name="ASPECT">{{#invoke:cite|journal|author1=Aspect, Alain |author2=Dalibard, Jean |author3=Roger, Gérard |date=December 1982 |title=Experimental Test of Bell's Inequalities Using Time- Varying Analyzers |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=49 |issue=25| pages=1804–1807| doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.49.1804| bibcode=1982PhRvL..49.1804A|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name='Bohr1935'>{{#invoke:cite|journal|title=Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality be Considered Complete? |date=October 13, 1935 |first=N. |last=Bohr |journal=[[Physical Review]] |volume=48 |issue=8 |pages=696–702 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.48.696|bibcode=1935PhRv...48..696B |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1060284/files/PhysRev.48.696.pdf |doi-access=free}}</ref>
* [[Ice#Friction properties|The slipperiness of ice]] is not due to [[Pressure melting point|pressure melting]]. While it is true that increased pressure, such as that exerted by someone standing on a sheet of ice, will lower the melting point of ice, experiments show that the effect is too weak to account for the lowered friction. [[Materials science|Materials scientists]] still debate whether [[Premelting#Ice skating|premelting or the heat of friction]] is the dominant cause of ice's slipperiness.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|journal|title=Pressure melting and ice skating |vauthors=Colbeck SC |journal=American Journal of Physics |volume=63 |page=888 |date=1995 |issue=10 |quote=Pressure melting cannot be responsible for the low friction of ice. The pressure needed to reach the melting temperature is above the compressive failure stress..." |doi=10.1119/1.18028|bibcode=1995AmJPh..63..888C}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|title=Explaining Ice: The Answers Are Slippery |author=Kenneth Chang |date=Feb 21, 2006 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/02/21/science/21ice.html |url-access=subscription |work=The New York Times |quote=According to the frequently cited — if incorrect — explanation of why ice is slippery under an ice skate, the pressure exerted along the blade lowers the melting temperature of the top layer of ice, the ice melts and the blade glides on a thin layer of water that refreezes to ice as soon as the blade passes... But the explanation fails... because the pressure-melting effect is small.}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|journal|author=Robert Rosenberg |url=https://www.asc.ohio-state.edu/jayaprakash.1/846/skating.pdf |date=December 2005 |title=Why is Ice slippery? |journal=Physics Today |pages=50–55}}</ref><ref name="Bl">{{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Bluhm |first=H. |author2=T. Inoue |author3=M. Salmeron |date=2000 |title=Friction of ice measured using lateral force microscopy |journal=Phys. Rev. B |volume=61 |issue=11 |page=7760 |bibcode=2000PhRvB..61.7760B |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.61.7760 |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1233739}}</ref>

== Psychology and neuroscience ==
* [[Cannabis in pregnancy|Cannabis use in pregnancy]] is not low risk. The tetrahydrocannabinol ([[THC]]) within cannabis crosses the placenta, directly exposing the developing fetus to this chemical. Cannabis use in pregnancy is linked to increased risk of preterm delivery and lower birth weight, along with a higher likelihood of infants needing placement in the neonatal intensive care unit.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gunn |first1=J. K. L. |last2=Rosales |first2=C. B. |last3=Center |first3=K. E. |last4=Nuñez |first4=A. |last5=Gibson |first5=S. J. |last6=Christ |first6=C. |last7=Ehiri |first7=J. E. |date=2016-04-01 |title=Prenatal exposure to cannabis and maternal and child health outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=[[BMJ Open]] |language=en |volume=6 |issue=4 |article-number=e009986 |doi=10.1136/bmjopen-2015-009986 |doi-access=free|issn=2044-6055 |pmid=27048634 |pmc=4823436}}</ref> Additionally, infants exposed to cannabis in pregnancy may have increased rates of behavioral conditions such as hyperactivity and impulsivity, attention deficits, sleep disorders, emotional disturbances, and a higher chance of substance use.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Renard |first1=Justine |last2=Konefal |first2=Sarah |date=2022 |title=Clearing the Smoke on Cannabis: Cannabis Use During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding - An Update |url=https://www.ccsa.ca/sites/default/files/2022-05/CCSA-Cannabis-Use-Pregnancy-Breastfeeding-Report-2022-en.pdf |journal=Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction}}</ref> According to a 2015 study, 70% of pregnant American women that had used marijuana in the past year thought that consumption of cannabis once or twice per week carried low to no risk of general harm.<ref name="pmid25772211">{{cite journal |author=Ko JY |author2=Farr SL |author3=Tong VT |author4=Creanga AA |author5=Callaghan WM |title=Prevalence and patterns of marijuana use among pregnant and nonpregnant women of reproductive age. |journal=[[American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology]] |year=2015 |volume=213 |issue=2 |pages=201.e1–201.e10 |pmid=25772211 |doi=10.1016/j.ajog.2015.03.021 |pmc=7469257}}</ref>
* True [[photographic memory]] (the ability to remember endless images, particularly pages or numbers, with such a high degree of precision that the image mimics a photo) has never been demonstrated to exist in any individual,<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|title=Photographic Memory |url=http://indianapublicmedia.org/amomentofscience/photographic-memory/|publisher=indianapublicmedia.org |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140427082738/http://indianapublicmedia.org/amomentofscience/photographic-memory/ |archive-date=April 27, 2014|url-status=live}}</ref> although a small number of young children have [[eidetic memory]], where they can recall an object with high precision for a few minutes after it is no longer present.<ref name="Simola">{{#invoke:cite|book |author=Anthony Simola |title=The Roving Mind: A Modern Approach to Cognitive Enhancement |publisher=ST Press |isbn=978-0-692-40905-3 |year=2015 |page=117 |access-date=May 10, 2016 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p4ZMBwAAQBAJ&pg=PT117}}</ref> Many people have claimed to have a photographic memory, but those people have been shown to have high precision memories as a result of [[mnemonic]] devices rather than a natural capacity for detailed memory encoding.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.slate.com/id/2140685/ |title=Kaavya Syndrome: The accused Harvard plagiarist doesn't have a photographic memory. No one does |author=Foer, Joshua |date=April 27, 2006 |work=Slate |access-date=January 20, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110924094531/http://www.slate.com/id/2140685 |archive-date=September 24, 2011 |url-status=live}}</ref> There are rare cases of individuals with [[exceptional memory]], but none of them have a memory that mimics that of a camera.
* The phase of the Moon does not influence fertility, cause a fluctuation in crime, or affect the stock market. There is no correlation between the [[Lunar effect|lunar cycle]] and human biology or behavior. However, the increased amount of illumination during the full moon may account for increased epileptic episodes, motorcycle accidents, or sleep disorders.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|journal |last1=Martens |first1=R. |last2=Kelly |first2=I. W. |last3=Saklofske |first3=D. H. |date=December 1988 |title=Lunar Phase and Birthrate: A 50-Year Critical Review |journal=[[Psychological Reports]] |volume=63 |issue=3 |pages=923–934 |doi=10.2466/pr0.1988.63.3.923 |pmid=3070616 |s2cid=34184527}}
<br />b. {{#invoke:cite|journal |last1=Rotton |first1=James |last2=Kelly |first2=I. W. |date=1985 |title=Much ado about the full moon: A meta-analysis of lunar-lunacy research |journal=[[Psychological Bulletin]] |volume=97 |issue=2 |pages=286–306 |doi=10.1037/0033-2909.97.2.286 |pmid=3885282}}
<br />c. {{Citation |last1=Kelly |first1=Ivan |title=The Moon Was Full and Nothing Happened: A Review of Studies on the Moon and Human Behavior |date=1986 |journal=Skeptical Inquirer |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=129–43 |last2=Rotton |first2=James |last3=Culver |first3=Roger}}. Reprinted in ''The Hundredth Monkey – and other paradigms of the paranormal'', edited by [[Kendrick Frazier]], Prometheus Books. Revised and updated in ''The Outer Edge: Classic Investigations of the Paranormal'', edited by [[Joe Nickell]], [[Barry Karr]], and [[Tom Genoni]], 1996, [[CSICOP]].
<br />d. {{#invoke:cite|journal |last1=Foster |first1=Russell G. |last2=Roenneberg |first2=Till |date=2008 |title=Human Responses to the Geophysical Daily, Annual and Lunar Cycles |journal=[[Current Biology]] |volume=18 |issue=17 |pages=R784–R794 |bibcode=2008CBio...18.R784F |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2008.07.003 |pmid=18786384 |s2cid=15429616 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
* [[Repressed memory|Repressed memories]] (the latent, oftentimes traumatic memories of early childhood that are recalled later in life) do not exist. This idea may have been popularized by [[Marcel Proust]]'s ''[[In Search of Lost Time]].'' However, a person cannot retain memories from infancy. The localized amnesia of childhood trauma is impossible, although false memories can be induced.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Creating False Memories |url=https://staff.washington.edu/eloftus/Articles/sciam.htm |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=staff.washington.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Otgaar |first1=Henry |last2=Howe |first2=Mark L. |last3=Patihis |first3=Lawrence |last4=Merckelbach |first4=Harald |last5=Lynn |first5=Steven Jay |last6=Lilienfeld |first6=Scott O. |last7=Loftus |first7=Elizabeth F. |date=November 2019 |title=The Return of the Repressed: The Persistent and Problematic Claims of Long-Forgotten Trauma |journal=Perspectives on Psychological Science: A Journal of the Association for Psychological Science |volume=14 |issue=6 |pages=1072–1095 |doi=10.1177/1745691619862306 |issn=1745-6924 |pmc=6826861 |pmid=31584864}}</ref>

=== Mental disorders ===
* [[Vaccines and autism|Vaccines do not cause autism]]. There have been no successful attempts to reproduce [[MMR vaccine controversy|fraudulent research]] by British ex-doctor [[Andrew Wakefield]], where the misconception likely originates. Wakefield's research was ultimately shown to have been manipulated.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Godlee |first1=F. |last2=Smith |first2=J. |last3=Marcovitch |first3=H. |year=2011 |title=British Medical Journal: Wakefield's article linking MMR vaccine and autism was fraudulent |url=http://www.bmj.com/content/342/bmj.c7452.full |url-status=live |journal=BMJ |volume=342 |article-number=c7452 |doi=10.1136/bmj.c7452 |pmid=21209060 |s2cid=43640126 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131111093448/http://www.bmj.com/content/342/bmj.c7452.full |archive-date=November 11, 2013 |access-date=January 5, 2011}}</ref>
* [[Dyslexia]] is not defined or diagnosed as [[mirror writing]] or reading letters or words backwards.<ref name="LilienfeldLynn2011">{{#invoke:cite|book|last1=Lilienfeld |first1=Scott O. |author-link1=Scott Lilienfeld |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8DlS0gfO_QUC&pg=PT88 |title=50 Great Myths of Popular Psychology: Shattering Widespread Misconceptions about Human Behavior |last2=Lynn |first2=Steven Jay |last3=Ruscio |first3=John |last4=Beyerstein |first4=Barry L. |author-link4=Barry Beyerstein |date=15 September 2011 |publisher=[[Wiley (publisher)|John Wiley & Sons]] |isbn=978-1-4443-6074-5 |pages=88–91 |access-date=19 May 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170109130327/https://books.google.com/books?id=8DlS0gfO_QUC&pg=PT88 |archive-date=9 January 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Handler2011">{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Handler |first1=Sheryl M |last2=Fierson |first2=Walter M |date=March 1, 2011 |title=Learning disabilities, dyslexia, and vision. |journal=Pediatrics |publisher=[[American Academy of Pediatrics]] |volume=127 |issue=3 |pages=e820 |doi=10.1542/peds.2010-3670 |pmid=21357342 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Mirror writing and reading letters or words backwards are behaviors seen in many children (dyslexic or not) as they learn to read and write.<ref name="LilienfeldLynn2011"/><ref name="Handler2011"/> [[Dyslexia]] is a neurodevelopmental disorder of people who have at least average intelligence and who have difficulty in reading and writing that is not otherwise explained by low intelligence.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|last=Dinelli |first=Beth |title=Common Misconceptions about Dyslexia |url=https://www.commlearn.com/common-misconceptions-about-dyslexia/ |access-date=August 2, 2019 |website=Commonwealth Learning Center}}</ref>
* [[Self-harm]] is not generally an [[attention-seeking]] behavior. People who engage in self-harm are typically very self-conscious of their wounds and scars and feel guilty about their behavior, leading them to go to great lengths to conceal it from others.<ref name="MHF">{{#invoke:cite|book|url=http://www.mentalhealth.org.uk/publications/?EntryId5=38712 |title=Truth Hurts Report |publisher=Mental Health Foundation |year=2006 |isbn=978-1-903645-81-9 |access-date=June 11, 2008}}</ref> They may offer alternative explanations for their injuries, or conceal their scars with clothing.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|author=Helen Spandler |title=Who's Hurting Who? Young people, self-harm and suicide |publisher=42nd Street |year=1996 |isbn=978-1-900782-00-5 |place=Manchester}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|url=https://archive.org/details/selfharmperspect0000unse |title=Self-harm – Perspectives from personal experience |publisher=Chipmunka/Survivors Speak Out |year=1994 |isbn=978-1-904697-04-6 |editor=Pembroke, L. R. |url-access=registration}}</ref>
* There is no evidence that a chemical imbalance or neurotransmitter deficiency is the sole factor in depression and other mental disorders, but rather a combination of biological, psychological, and social factors.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|last=Stahl |first=S. M. |title=Stahl's essential psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific basis and practical applications |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2021 |isbn=978-1-108-98585-7 |edition=5th |page=264}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|date=March 17, 2022 |title=The Myth of the Chemical Imbalance {{!}} Ronald Pies |url=https://return.life/2022/03/17/the-myth-of-the-chemical-imbalance/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221201222841/https://return.life/2022/03/17/the-myth-of-the-chemical-imbalance/ |archive-date=1 December 2022 |access-date=June 1, 2022 |website=Return}}</ref>
* [[Schizophrenia]] does not involve split or multiple personalities. It is characterized by continuous or relapsing episodes of psychosis. Major symptoms include hallucinations (typically hearing voices), delusions, paranoia, and disorganized thinking. Other symptoms include social withdrawal, decreased emotional expression, and apathy.<ref>Diagnostic and Statistical Manual 5th edition.</ref> The term was coined from the Greek roots ''schizein'' and ''phrēn'', "to split" and "mind", in reference to a "splitting of mental functions" seen in schizophrenia, not a splitting of the personality.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|book|author=Baucum, Don |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iCVSdYdA36EC&pg=PA182 |title=Psychology |publisher=Barron's |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-7641-3421-0 |edition=2nd |location=Hauppauge, NY |page=182}}</ref> A split or multiple personality is [[dissociative identity disorder]].<ref name="MultiplePersonalities">a. {{#invoke:cite|web|title=Schizophrenia |url=http://www.nami.org/Template.cfm?Section=Schizophrenia9&Template=/ContentManagement/ContentDisplay.cfm&ContentID=118290 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120504155431/http://www.nami.org/Template.cfm?Section=Schizophrenia9&Template=%2FContentManagement%2FContentDisplay.cfm&ContentID=118290 |archive-date=May 4, 2012 |publisher=National Alliance on Mental Illness}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|title=10 Myths About Mental Illness |url=http://www.mha-oc.org/10myths.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110519221144/http://www.mha-oc.org/10myths.html |archive-date=May 19, 2011 |url-status=usurped |publisher=Mental Health Association}}</ref>

=== Brain ===
* Broad generalizations are often made in popular psychology about certain brain functions being [[Lateralization of brain function|lateralized]], or more predominant in one hemisphere than the other. [[Lateralization_of_brain_function#Misconceptions|These claims]] are often inaccurate or overstated.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Goswami |first1=U |title=Neuroscience and education: from research to practice? |journal=[[Nature Reviews. Neuroscience]] |volume=7 |issue=5 |pages=406–11 |date=2006 |pmid=16607400 |doi=10.1038/nrn1907 |s2cid=3113512}}</ref>
* The human brain, particularly the [[prefrontal cortex]], does not reach [[Neuroplasticity|"full maturity" or "full development"]] at [[The "brain matures at 25" myth|any particular age (e.g. 16, 18, 21, 25, 30).]] Changes in structure and [[myelination]] of [[gray matter]] are recorded to continue with relative consistency all throughout life including until death. Different mental abilities peak earlier or later in life.<ref>a. More modern research suggests that the prefrontal cortex region of the brain is changing in structure even well past the age of 30.{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Hartshorne |first1=Joshua K. |last2=Germine |first2=Laura T. |title=When Does Cognitive Functioning Peak? The Asynchronous Rise and Fall of Different Cognitive Abilities Across the Life Span |journal=Psychological Science |date=April 2015 |volume=26 |issue=4 |pages=433–443 |doi=10.1177/0956797614567339 |pmid=25770099 |pmc=4441622 |quote="Some abilities peak and begin to decline around high school graduation; some abilities plateau in early adulthood, beginning to decline in subjects' 30s; and still others do not peak until subjects reach their 40s or later. These findings motivate a nuanced theory of maturation and age-related decline, in which multiple, dissociable factors differentially affect different domains of cognition."}}
b. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.menshealth.com/health/a26868313/when-does-your-brain-fully-mature/ |title=People's Brains Don't Reach Adulthood Until Age 30, Study Finds|website=Men's Health|first=MEelissa|last=Matthews |date=March 19, 2019|quote="What we're really saying is that to have a definition of when you move from childhood to adulthood looks increasingly absurd... It's a much more nuanced transition that takes place over three decades."}}<br/>
c. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/science/adult-brain-30s-teenagers-crime-mental-health-research-a8828681.html |title=Scientists think you are not a proper adult until you enter your 30s |website=[[Independent.co.uk]] |date=March 18, 2019}}<br/>
d. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/health/news/8204782/Brain-only-fully-matures-in-middle-age-claims-neuroscientist.html#:~:text=You%20might%20think%20that%20you,developing%20until%20your%20late%2040s.&text=Scientists%20used%20to%20believe%20that,changing%20well%20into%20middle%20age | title=Brain only fully 'matures' in middle age, claims neuroscientist| date=December 16, 2010}}<br/>
e. {{#invoke:cite|journal|doi=10.1073/pnas.1105108108 |title=Extraordinary neoteny of synaptic spines in the human prefrontal cortex |year=2011 |last1=Petanjek |first1=Zdravko |last2=Judaš |first2=Miloš |last3=Šimić |first3=Goran |last4=Rašin |first4=Mladen Roko |last5=Uylings |first5=Harry B. M. |last6=Rakic |first6=Pasko |last7=Kostović |first7=Ivica |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=108 |issue=32 |pages=13281–13286 |pmid=21788513 |pmc=3156171 |bibcode=2011PNAS..10813281P |doi-access=free}}<br/>
f. {{cite magazine |url=https://slate.com/human-interest/2020/01/age-of-consent-25-advice.html |title=My Progressive Friends Say It's Immoral to Have Sex With Anyone Under 25 |first=Stoya |last=Juzwiak |author2=Rich Juzwiak |date=January 9, 2020 |magazine=Slate}}<br/>
g. {{#invoke:cite|news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/08/22/magazine/22Adulthood-t.html|title=What Is It About 20-Somethings?|newspaper=The New York Times|first=Robin Marantz |last=Henig|date=August 18, 2010}}<br/>
h. {{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Cockcroft |first1=Kate |title=The role of working memory in childhood education: Five questions and answers |journal=South African Journal of Childhood Education |date=4 September 2015 |volume=5 |issue=1 |page=18 |id={{ProQuest|1898641293}} |doi=10.4102/sajce.v5i1.347 |doi-access=free}}<br/>

The Asynchronous Rise and Fall of Different Cognitive Abilities Across the Life Span |journal=Psychological Science |date=April 2015 |volume=26 |issue=4 |pages=433–443 |doi=10.1177/0956797614567339 |pmid=25770099 |pmc=4441622}}<br/>
j. {{#invoke:cite|web|last=Hu |first=Jane C. |date=2022-11-28 |title=A Powerful Idea About Our Brains Stormed Pop Culture and Captured Minds. It's Mostly Bunk. |url=https://slate.com/technology/2022/11/brain-development-25-year-old-mature-myth.html |access-date=2022-11-28 |website=Slate Magazine |language=en}}</ref>
* [[File:Gyrus Dentatus 40x.jpg|thumb|Some neurons can reform in the human brain.]] Humans do not generate all of the brain cells they will ever have by the age of two years. Although this belief was held by medical experts until 1998, it is now understood that new [[neuron]]s can be created [[postnatal|after infancy]] in some parts of the brain into late adulthood.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal| author = Gross C. G. | date = 2000 |title=Neurogenesis in the adult brain: death of a dogma | journal = Nat Rev Neurosci | volume = 1 | issue = 1| pages = 67–73 | doi = 10.1038/35036235| pmid = 11252770 | s2cid = 2347812}}</ref>
* People do not use [[Ten percent of the brain myth|only 10% of their brains]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.snopes.com/science/stats/10percent.asp|title=Snopes on brains|website=[[Snopes]]|date=February 8, 2000 |access-date=August 29, 2009}}</ref><ref name="Radford 1999">{{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Radford|first=Benjamin|date=March–April 1999|title=The Ten-Percent Myth|journal=Skeptical Inquirer|issn=0194-6730|url=http://www.csicop.org/si/show/the_ten-percent_myth/|access-date=April 15, 2009|quote=It's the old myth heard time and again about how people use only ten percent of their brains |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131030034901/http://www.csicop.org/si/show/the_ten-percent_myth/ |archive-date=October 30, 2013| url-status=live}}</ref> While it is true that a small minority of [[neuron]]s in the brain are actively firing at any one time, a healthy human will normally use most of their brain over the course of a day, and the inactive neurons are important as well. The idea that activating 100% of the brain would allow someone to achieve their maximum potential and/or gain various psychic abilities is common in [[Ten percent of the brain myth#In popular culture|folklore and fiction]],<ref name="Radford 1999"/><ref name="beyersteinbrain"/><ref name="msnbc news ref">{{#invoke:cite|web|last=Bahn |first=Christopher |title='Limitless' brainpower plot isn't all that crazy |work=TODAY.com |date=7 March 2011 |url=http://today.msnbc.msn.com/id/41953704/ns/today-entertainment/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110313105800/http://today.msnbc.msn.com/id/41953704/ns/today-entertainment/ |archive-date=March 13, 2011 |access-date=March 31, 2011}}</ref> but doing so in real life would likely result in a fatal [[seizure]].<ref name="Fish2014">{{#invoke:cite|journal|vauthors=Fisher RS, Acevedo C, Arzimanoglou A, Bogacz A, Cross JH, Elger CE, Engel J, Forsgren L, French JA, Glynn M, Hesdorffer DC, Lee BI, Mathern GW, Moshé SL, Perucca E, Scheffer IE, Tomson T, Watanabe M, Wiebe S |date=April 2014 |title=ILAE official report: a practical clinical definition of epilepsy |journal=Epilepsia |volume=55 |issue=4 |pages=475–482 |doi=10.1111/epi.12550 |pmid=24730690 |doi-access=free |s2cid=35958237}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|news|date=February 13, 2018 |title=The Life and Times of the 10% Neuromyth – Knowing Neurons |language=en-GB |work=Knowing Neurons |url=https://knowingneurons.com/2018/02/13/10-neuromyth/ |url-status=live |access-date=February 24, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180315133927/https://knowingneurons.com/2018/02/13/10-neuromyth/ |archive-date=March 15, 2018}}</ref> This misconception was attributed to late 19th century leading thinker [[William James]], who apparently used the expression only metaphorically.<ref name="beyersteinbrain">{{#invoke:cite|book|last=Beyerstein|first=Barry L.|title=Mind Myths: Exploring Popular Assumptions About the Mind and Brain|editor=Sergio Della Sala |publisher=Wiley |date=1999 |pages=3–24 |chapter=Whence Cometh the Myth that We Only Use 10% of our Brains? |isbn=978-0-471-98303-3}}</ref>
* Although [[Phineas Gage]]'s brain injuries, caused by a several-foot-long tamping rod driven completely through his skull, caused him to become temporarily disabled, descriptions of his aberrant behavior in later life are disputed, contradicting other claims that he recovered fully.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Barker |first=F. G. II |year=1995 |url=http://mysois.uwm.edu/omeka/archive/files/b7cf786e3d97d4cf63ac3b7d14e1f88e.pdf |title=Phineas among the phrenologists: the American crowbar case and nineteenth-century theories of cerebral localization |journal=Journal of Neurosurgery |volume=82 |issue=4 |pages=672–82 |pmid=7897537 |doi=10.3171/jns.1995.82.4.0672 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006074853/http://mysois.uwm.edu/omeka/archive/files/b7cf786e3d97d4cf63ac3b7d14e1f88e.pdf |archive-date=October 6, 2014}}</ref>

=== Senses ===
[[File:Taste buds.svg|thumb|upright|An {{em|incorrect}} [[tongue map|map of the tongue]] showing taste zones. In fact, all zones can sense all tastes.]]
* Humans have more than the commonly cited five senses. The number of senses in various categorizations ranges from 5 to more than 20. In addition to sight, smell, taste, touch, and hearing, which were the senses identified by [[Aristotle]], humans can sense [[Balance (ability)|balance]] and acceleration ([[equilibrioception]]), pain ([[nociception]]), body and limb position ([[proprioception]] or kinesthetic sense), and relative temperature ([[thermoception]]).<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|author=Cerretani, Jessica |date=Spring 2010 |website=Harvard Medicine |publisher=Harvard College |url=http://harvardmedicine.hms.harvard.edu/fascinoma/fivesenses/beyond/extra.php |title=Extra Sensory Perceptions |access-date=January 13, 2011| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120211190433/http://harvardmedicine.hms.harvard.edu/fascinoma/fivesenses/beyond/extra.php |archive-date=February 11, 2012}}</ref> Other senses sometimes identified are the sense of time, [[Human echolocation|echolocation]], itching, pressure, hunger, thirst, fullness of the stomach, need to urinate, need to defecate, blood carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>) levels,<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://health.howstuffworks.com/mental-health/human-nature/perception/question242.htm |date=April 2000 |title=How many senses does a human being have? |website=Discovery Health |publisher=[[Discovery Communications Inc.]] |access-date=January 13, 2011 |archive-date=November 6, 2011 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20111106034223/http://health.howstuffworks.com/mental-health/human-nature/perception/question242.htm |url-status=live}}</ref> and electric field sensation.<ref name="Shimizu">{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Odagiri-Shimizu |first1=H |last2=Shimizu |first2=K |title=Experimental analysis of the human perception threshold of a DC electric field |journal=Medical * Biological Engineering & Computing |date=Nov 1999 |volume=37 |issue=6 |pages=727–732 |doi=10.1007/BF02513374 |pmid=10723879}}</ref>
* All different tastes can be detected on all parts of the tongue by taste buds,<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|title=The cells and logic for mammalian sour taste detection|journal=Nature|volume=442|issue=7105 |pages=934–938 |date=August 2006|pmid=16929298|pmc=1571047 |doi=10.1038/nature05084|bibcode=2006Natur.442..934H |vauthors=Huang AL, Chen X, Hoon MA, Chandrashekar J, Guo W, Tränkner D, Ryba NJ, Zuker CS}}</ref> with slightly increased sensitivities in different locations depending on the person; the [[tongue map]] showing the contrary is fallacious.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|date=October 22, 2002|title=Beyond the Tongue Map|publisher=Asha.org |url=http://www.asha.org/Publications/leader/2002/021022/f021022a.htm|access-date=August 29, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131214115137/http://www.asha.org/Publications/leader/2002/021022/f021022a.htm|archive-date=December 14, 2013}}</ref>
* There are not four [[primary tastes]], but five: in addition to bitter, sour, salty, and sweet, humans have taste receptors for [[umami]], which is a "savory" or "meaty" taste.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|book|title=Food Science and Technology |last=Campbell-Platt |first=Geoffrey |date=2009 |publisher=Wiley |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=E7GXHploJasC&pg=PA31 |isbn=978-0-632-06421-2 |page=31}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.rtc.edu/programs/generaleducation/biology/biology220/files/Senses_notes.pdf |title=Senses Notes |access-date=January 13, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110720040515/http://www.rtc.edu/programs/generaleducation/biology/biology220/files/Senses_notes.pdf |archive-date=July 20, 2011}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|web|author=Krulwich, Robert |date=November 5, 2007 |title=Sweet, Sour, Salty, Bitter&nbsp;... and Umami |url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=15819485 |website=Krulwich Wonders, an NPR Science Blog |publisher=NPR |access-date=January 13, 2011}}
<br/>d. {{Cite web |title=Probing Question: What is umami? {{!}} Penn State University |url=https://www.psu.edu/news/research/story/probing-question-what-umami/ |access-date=2024-07-23 |website=www.psu.edu |date=31 March 2015 |language=en}}</ref> Fat does interact with specific [[Receptor (biochemistry)|receptors]] in [[taste bud]] cells, but whether it is a sixth primary taste remains inconclusive.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Besnard|first=P |date=December 2015|title=Taste of Fat: A Sixth Taste Modality?|journal=Physiological Reviews|volume=96|issue=1 |pages=151–176|doi=10.1152/physrev.00002.2015|pmid=26631596 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
* The human [[sense of smell]] is not weak or underdeveloped. Humans have similar senses of smell to other mammals, and are more sensitive to some odors than rodents and dogs.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last=McGann |first=John P. |date=2017-05-12 |title=Poor human olfaction is a 19th-century myth |journal=Science |language=en |volume=356 |issue=6338 |article-number=eaam7263 |doi=10.1126/science.aam7263 |issn=0036-8075 |pmc=5512720 |pmid=28495701 |bibcode=2017Sci...356m7263M}}</ref>

== Toxicology ==
* [[Smokeless tobacco]] is not a "safe" alternative to conventional tobacco; smokeless tobacco products contain [[nicotine]] and are therefore highly addictive.<ref name="VidyasagaranSiddiqi2016">{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Vidyasagaran |first1=A. L. |last2=Siddiqi |first2=K. |last3=Kanaan |first3=M. |year=2016 |title=Use of smokeless tobacco and risk of cardiovascular disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis |url=http://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/101100/1/EJPC_D_16_00085_R1_2016.pdf |journal=European Journal of Preventive Cardiology |volume=23 |issue=18 |pages=1970–1981 |doi=10.1177/2047487316654026 |issn=2047-4873 |pmid=27256827 |s2cid=206820997}}</ref> They also can cause various harmful effects such as dental disease, [[oral cancer]], [[Esophageal cancer|oesophagus cancer]], and [[Pancreatic cancer|pancreas cancer]], [[Coronary artery disease|coronary heart disease]], as well as negative reproductive effects including [[stillbirth]], [[premature birth]] and [[low birth weight]].<ref name="VidyasagaranSiddiqi2016"/><ref name="Gupta 2019">{{#invoke:cite|journal|last1=Gupta |first1=Ruchika |last2=Gupta |first2=Sanjay |last3=Sharma |first3=Shashi |last4=Sinha |first4=Dhirendra N |last5=Mehrotra |first5=Ravi |date=2019-01-01 |title=Risk of Coronary Heart Disease Among Smokeless Tobacco Users: Results of Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Global Data |url=https://academic.oup.com/ntr/article/21/1/25/4793346 |journal=Nicotine & Tobacco Research |language=en |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=25–31 |doi=10.1093/ntr/nty002 |issn=1469-994X |pmc=6941711 |pmid=29325111}}</ref>
* Swallowing gasoline does not generally require special emergency treatment, as long as it goes into the stomach and not the lungs. This does {{em|not}} mean gasoline is safe to drink; it is very dangerous when consumed.<ref>{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |date=June 1995 |title=Toxicalogical Profile for Gasoline |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK594148/ |website=National Center for Biotechnology Information |publisher= |access-date=24 January 2026}}</ref> Inducing vomiting can make it worse.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://healthcare.utah.edu/the-scope/shows.php?shows=0_g9tzppx4 |publisher=[[University of Utah]]|title= Dos and Don'ts in Case of Gasoline Poisoning |author=University of Utah Poison Control Center|date=June 24, 2014}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|url= https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/MMG/MMG.asp?id=465&tid=83 |title= Medical Management Guidelines for Gasoline (Mixture) CAS# 86290-81-5 and 8006-61-9 |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] |date= October 21, 2014 |author= Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry |author-link= Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry}}</ref>
* A [[chloroform]]-soaked rag cannot instantly incapacitate a person.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|last=Payne|first=J. P.|s2cid=1718276|date=July 1998|title=The criminal use of chloroform|journal=[[Anaesthesia (journal)|Anaesthesia]]|volume=53|issue=7|pages=685–690|doi=10.1046/j.1365-2044.1998.528-az0572.x|pmid=9771177|doi-access=free}}</ref> It takes at least five minutes of inhaling an item soaked in chloroform to render a person unconscious. Most criminal cases involving chloroform also involve another drug being co-administered, such as alcohol or [[diazepam]], or the victim being found to have been complicit in its administration. The misconception that chloroform can be used as an [[incapacitating agent]]<ref>{{#invoke:cite|journal|title=Medical Annotation: Chloroform amongst Thieves |journal=[[The Lancet]] |date=1865 |volume=2 |issue=2200 |pages=490–491|doi=10.1016/s0140-6736(02)58434-8}}</ref> has been popularized by crime fiction authors.
* Although bananas contain naturally occurring [[radioactive isotope]]s, particularly [[potassium-40]] (<sup>40</sup>K), which emit [[ionizing radiation]] when undergoing [[radioactive decay]], the levels of such radiation are far too low to induce [[radiation poisoning]], and bananas are not a radiation hazard. It would not be physically possible to eat enough bananas to cause radiation poisoning, as [[Cumulative dose|the radiation dose from bananas is non-cumulative]].<ref name="AdventHealth 2018">{{#invoke:cite|web|title=The Most Common Medical Radiation Myths Dispelled |url=https://www.ahu.edu/blog/the-most-common-medical-radiation-myths-dispelled |access-date=2022-11-05 |website=AdventHealth University |date=May 21, 2018 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Loughran 2022">{{#invoke:cite|web|last=Loughran |first=Sarah |title=Are bananas really 'radioactive'? An expert clears up common misunderstandings about radiation |url=http://theconversation.com/are-bananas-really-radioactive-an-expert-clears-up-common-misunderstandings-about-radiation-193211 |access-date=2022-11-06 |website=The Conversation |date=November 3, 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|book|last1=Eisenbud |first1=Merril |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=67Pn4ydLOVAC |title=Environmental radioactivity: from natural, industrial, and military sources |last2=Gesell |first2=Thomas F. |publisher=Academic Press |year=1997 |isbn=978-0-12-235154-9 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=67Pn4ydLOVAC&pg=PA171 171–172] |quote=It is important to recognize that the potassium content of the body is under strict homeostatic control and is not influenced by variations in environmental levels. For this reason, the dose from {{sup|40}}K in the body is constant.}}
<br/>b. U. S. Environmental Protection Agency (1999), [https://web.archive.org/web/20210925200857/https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-05/documents/402-r-99-001.pdf Federal Guidance Report 13], page 16: "For example, the ingestion coefficient risk for 40K would not be appropriate for an application to ingestion of <sup>40</sup>K in conjunction with an elevated intake of natural potassium. This is because the biokinetic model for potassium used in this document represents the relatively slow removal of potassium (biological half-time 30 days) that is estimated to occur for typical intakes of potassium, whereas an elevated intake of potassium would result in excretion of a nearly equal mass of natural potassium, and hence of <sup>40</sup>K, over a short period."
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|web|author=Maggie Koerth-Baker |author-link=Maggie Koerth-Baker |date=Aug 27, 2010 |title=Bananas are radioactive—But they aren't a good way to explain radiation exposure |url=http://boingboing.net/2010/08/27/bananas-are-radioact.html |access-date=25 May 2011}}. Attributes the title statement to Geoff Meggitt, former UK Atomic Energy Authority.</ref> (See also: [[Banana equivalent dose]])
* Ingesting [[Visine]], a brand of eye drops, does not cause diarrhea. It is [[Neurotoxicity|neurotoxic]], with consumption causing several serious side effects. Pranks spiking people with Visine rose after the misconception was popularized by the film ''[[Wedding Crashers]]''.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|news|date=July 24, 2013 |title=Nothing funny about so-called 'Visine prank,' says pharmacist |url=https://www.therecord.com/news/waterloo-region/nothing-funny-about-so-called-visine-prank-says-pharmacist/article_c955e29f-ffab-5c9b-a82f-671ff7ea9dc3.html |work=[[Waterloo Region Record]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Blum |first=Deborah |date=March 25, 2013 |title=Just an (Eye) Drop of Poison |url=https://www.wired.com/2013/03/just-an-eye-drop-of-poison/ |magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]}}</ref>

== Transportation ==

[[File:Bermuda Triangle.png|thumb|One version of the Bermuda Triangle area]]
* The [[Bermuda Triangle]] does not have any more shipwrecks or mysterious disappearances than most other waterways.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|news|url =https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-22806362|title =Study finds shipwrecks threaten precious seas|date =June 7, 2013|access-date = June 7, 2013|publisher =BBC News/science}}

<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|journal| url=https://www.csmonitor.com/Science/2013/0610/Bermuda-Triangle-doesn-t-make-the-cut-on-list-of-world-s-most-dangerous-oceans | title=Bermuda Triangle doesn't make the cut on list of world's most dangerous oceans | journal=The Christian Science Monitor | access-date=March 22, 2016| date=June 10, 2013}}
<br/>c. {{#invoke:cite|book|title=The Bermuda Triangle Mystery Solved| year=1975|first=Lawrence David|last= Kusche|isbn = 978-0-87975-971-1|publisher=Prometheus Books|location = Buffalo, NY|ref=Kusche, 1975}}</ref>
* Toilet waste is never intentionally jettisoned from a commercial aircraft. All waste is collected in tanks and emptied into [[Ground support equipment#Lavatory service vehicles|toilet waste vehicles]].<ref>{{#invoke:cite|web|url =https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/airplanes-dump-waste-in-flight/|title =Do Airplane Toilets Dump Waste While in Flight?|date =Dec 17, 2022|access-date = July 1, 2025|publisher =Snopes}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:cite|news|url=https://blogs.wsj.com/middleseat/2008/11/19/on-world-toilet-day-let-us-praise-the-airline-lav/|last=Philips|first=Matt|title=On World Toilet Day, Let Us Praise the Airline Lav|work=The Middle Seat Terminal (Wall Street Journal)|access-date=April 2, 2009|date=November 19, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131214105710/https://blogs.wsj.com/middleseat/2008/11/19/on-world-toilet-day-let-us-praise-the-airline-lav/ |archive-date=December 14, 2013| url-status=live}}</ref> [[Blue ice (aviation)|Blue ice]] is caused by accidental leakage from the waste tank. [[Passenger train toilet]]s, on the other hand, have indeed historically flushed onto the tracks, and the practice still exists in some countries. Modern trains in most developed countries usually have retention tanks on board and therefore do not dispose of waste in such a manner.
* [[automotive battery|Automotive batteries]] stored on a concrete floor do not discharge any faster than they would on other surfaces, in spite of a worry that concrete harms batteries.<ref name="Snopes">{{#invoke:cite|web|url=http://www.snopes.com/autos/techno/battery.asp|title=Battery Parked|work=[[Snopes]]|date=February 8, 2011|access-date=June 2, 2013}}</ref> Early batteries with porous, leaky cases may have been susceptible to moisture from floors, but for many years [[Lead–acid battery|lead–acid car batteries]] have had impermeable [[polypropylene]] cases.<ref>{{#invoke:cite|news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=k8BIAAAAIBAJ&pg=2232,1623674|title= No End to Battery Storage Debate|newspaper=The Vindicator |date= November 4, 1999|first1=Tom|last1=Magliozzi|author1-link= Tom Magliozzi|first2= Ray|last2= Magliozzi|author2-link=Ray Magliozzi|page=37}}</ref> While most modern automotive batteries are [[VRLA battery|sealed]], and do not leak battery acid when properly stored and maintained,<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|book|title=Ask Click and Clack: Answers from Car Talk|first1=Tom|last1= Magliozzi|author1-link=Tom Magliozzi|first2=Ray|last2=Magliozzi|author2-link=Ray Magliozzi|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=Z1nntWoIBp4C&pg=PA68|pages=68–69|publisher=Chronicle Books|date=2008|isbn= 978-0-8118-6477-0 |access-date= June 2, 2013}}
<br/>b. {{cite magazine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MxXlKb9wIe0C&pg=PA136 |title=Car Care Auto Clinic |magazine=[[Popular Mechanics]] |date=November 2000 |volume=177 |issue=11 |issn=0032-4558 |page=136 |access-date=June 2, 2013}}</ref> the sulfuric acid in them can leak out and stain, etch, or corrode concrete floors if their cases crack or tip over or their vent-holes are breached by floods.<ref>a. {{#invoke:cite|news|title=Use care in cleaning battery-acid stain|url=https://www.seattletimes.com/life/lifestyle/use-care-in-cleaning-battery-acid-stain/|first=Karen|last=Youso|website=The Seattle Times|access-date=May 9, 2018|date=October 4, 2008}}
<br/>b. {{#invoke:cite|web|title=Managing Used Lead-Acid Batteries|url=http://www.gecap.org/pdf/lead-acid_batteries.pdf|website=Georgia Environmental Compliance Assistance Program|publisher=Georgia Tech Research Institute|access-date=May 9, 2018|date=July 2002|archive-date=October 28, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201028080456/https://www.gecap.org/pdf/lead-acid_batteries.pdf}}</ref>

== Weapons ==

* Someone hit by a shotgun will not [[Stopping power#Knockback|fly backwards]] like it is often portrayed in movies, and the same is true for other handheld weapons. The [[momentum]] of the bullet is no higher than the [[recoil]] transmitted to the shooter, which is too little to cause any significant motion.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Karger|first1=B.|last2=Kneubuehl|first2=B. P.|date=1996|title=On the physics of momentum in ballistics: can the human body be displaced or knocked down by a small arms projectile?|journal=International Journal of Legal Medicine|volume=109|issue=3|pages=147–149|doi=10.1007/BF01369676|issn=0937-9827|pmid=8956990}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-10-06 |title=Top 13 Firearm Myths &#038; Misconceptions |url=https://www.pewpewtactical.com/firearm-myths-misconceptions/ |access-date=2026-06-01 |website=www.pewpewtactical.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

* [[Land mine]]s explode immediately when stepped on. They are not armed when stepped on and then triggered by stepping off, as depicted in fictional portrayals where disarming the mine is a source of narrative.<ref>{{Cite book |last=United Nations Mine Action Service (UNMAS) |url=https://unmas.org/sites/default/files/handbook_english.pdf |title=Landmines, Explosive Remnants of War and IED Safety Handbook |year=2015 |edition=3rd |pages=61–64}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author=Ju Shardlow and David Ibekwe |title=Special forces bomb disposal expert rates 10 bomb disposal scenes in movies and TV |url=https://www.insider.com/sas-bomb-disposal-expert-rates-bomb-disposal-scenes-in-movies-2020-9 |publisher=Insider |date=2020-11-11}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Brutsch |first=Alexandra |date=2023-10-06 |title=Landmine goes click? |url=https://fsd.ch/en/landmine-goes-click/ |access-date=2026-06-10 |website=FSD.CH |language=en-GB}}</ref>
